Session Name: NFBC1A (ACCEPTED APPLICANTS ONLY) New Faculty Boot Camp - Friday
Description:
*** ACCEPTED APPLICANTS ONLY *** 

The NFBC is designed for members-in-training, including clinical fellows in the final two years of their training and PhD post-doctoral fellows in the final three years of their training.  In addition, early-career faculty within the first three years of their initial faculty appointment, regardless of doctoral degree, are eligible to apply.  Applicants should be actively engaged in basic, translational, clinical, epidemiological, or health systems research, medical education, or other academic activities in pulmonary, critical care, or sleep medicine.  Selected participants will be invited to attend a two-day course featuring recognized experts who will provide insights and strategies to overcome the unique challenges faced during the transition from trainee to faculty. 

The overarching goal of the program is to equip participants with actionable strategies for navigating the challenging transition from clinical fellowships or Ph.D. post-doctoral training to independent positions as academic faculty.  We offer three main tracks within the program to cater to specific careers: PhD scientist, clinician educator, and clinician scientist.  The NFBC is an intensive and immersive program that offers a fantastic opportunity for networking with leaders in the field and similar-minded colleagues and peers and aims to provide critical information not often covered during training.  We encourage PhD scientists, clinician educators, and clinician scientists to apply to this outstanding program!  The following text describes the specifics of each career track that is included in the NFBC.

Session Name: PG2 ULTRASOUND UNLOCKED: ADVANCING ULTRASOUND PRACTICE AND INSTRUCTION
Description: This interactive session is designed for clinicians and educators seeking to reinforce basic point of care ultrasound skills for acutely ill patients. Participants will review diagnostic protocols, refine image acquisition and interpretation techniques with live models, and review tips and tricks of ultrasonography with expert faculty. The session will also focus on practical strategies for using and teaching ultrasound effectively, addressing common pitfalls, ergonomic techniques, and learner engagement across experience levels. This course bridges clinical application and education, equipping participants to both perform and teach high-quality ultrasound at the bedside.

Session Name: PG6 BEST PRACTICES IN PULMONARY FUNCTION TESTING
Description: This course focuses on clinical lung function testing, integrating recent technical standards and interpretive strategies with interactive, small-group learning. Participants will engage in didactic lectures, case-based instruction, and live demonstrations of pulmonary function testing (PFT). A multidisciplinary team—including clinicians, respiratory therapists, and lab directors—will guide discussions. Emphasis will be placed on race-neutral equations in PFT, reflecting evolving literature. The course concludes with expert panel discussions of complex cases, offering diverse perspectives and practical insights into PFT performance, interpretation, and reporting.

Session Name: PG9 STATE OF THE ART: LUNG CANCER IN 2026
Description: This course will provide a comprehensive review of topics in the evaluation and management of patients with known and suspected lung cancer. We will discuss recent developments in the areas of tobacco control, updated guidelines for lung cancer staging, advances in lung cancer screening, invasive diagnostic approaches for patients with lung nodules and mediastinal staging, biomarkers across the spectrum of lung cancer, and updates in multimodal treatment approaches for lung cancer. Attention will be given to global variations and potential disparities across the lung cancer continuum. Interactive tumor boards will be held to highlight these topics and encourage participant engagement.

Session Name: PG8 BRONCHIECTASIS AND NTM PULMONARY DISEASE: ETIOLOGIES, COMPLEX CASE MANAGEMENT, AND UPDATED GUIDELINES
Description: The diagnosis and management of bronchiectasis and nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) pulmonary infections are challenging due to the complexity of these chronic lung diseases and limited evidence-based management strategies. There have fortunately been multiple significant advances, and this session will provide learners on the evolving landscape. Topics include current epidemiology, environmental risk factors, pathophysiology, and diagnostic considerations. The session will review new bronchiectasis management guidelines expected in late 2025 and explore novel approaches being pursued in active clinical trials. Through a combination of didactic presentations and expert panel discussions, participants will gain practical insights to enhance patient care and clinical decision-making.

Description: The International Poster Colloquium (IPC) is a signature event of the ATS International Conference, designed to showcase high-quality research and innovative programs from around the world. The colloquium provides an interactive forum where international scholars and clinicians present their work, engage in discussion with peers and senior faculty, and receive feedback from expert moderators. Session Name: PG14 CARDIOPULMONARY EXERCISE TESTING: ADVANCES AND APPLICATIONS
Description: This course focuses on the cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET). This includes education on the physiologic basis for CPET, current guidelines, quality control and advances in CPET methods to assess the pulmonary system and central hemodynamics during exercise. Interpretative strategies and common CPET responses in disease states will be presented in didactic sessions and followed by practice-based learning in an interactive small group setting. Learners will be supported during practice-based learning by expert Faculty. The inclusion of a live CPET demonstration will complement the didactic sessions, and highlight the multidisciplinary components necessary for performing high-quality CPET.

Session Name: PG10 MECHANISTIC AND MULTIMODAL OSA TREATMENT: NERVE STIMULATION, SURGERY, ORAL APPLIANCES, AND EMERGING PHARMACOTHERAPY
Description: Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation (HNS), Oral Appliance (OA), Maxillary Mandibular Advancement (MMA) surgery, and pharmacotherapy are evidence-based positive airway pressure (PAP) treatment alternatives for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Dual GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonist and mechanistically targeted combination treatment (aroxybutynin and atomoxetine) are expected to become viable alternatives to PAP for selected patients. This session will review recent clinical evidence and technical advancements in non-PAP OSA therapies. Interactive case studies and hands-on workshops will provide participants with practical training in HNS titration, OA device selection, and adherence tracking technologies.

Session Name: PG12 SUPPORTING THE FAILING HEART: MCS AND VA-ECMO FOR THE PRACTICING INTENSIVIST
Description: There is a steady trend of increased use of mechanical circulatory support (MCS) and veno arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) for hemodynamic support in cardiogenic shock. Given the growing complexity of critically ill patients, an understanding of when to refer patients for MCS or ECMO, and how these support modalities work, is becoming essential for critical care providers. Despite this, resources and education for general intensivists are lacking. The goal of this session is to provide a broad overview of MCS ECMO for ICU providers, and to review the basic physiology, assessment, and troubleshooting of the three most common MCS modalities: VA-ECMO, Impellas, and intra-aortic balloon pumps.

Session Name: PG21 TRANSLATIONAL WINDOWS INTO THE LUNG MICROENVIRONMENT: ADVANCES WITH PRECISION-CUT LUNG SLICES
Description: The PG course on the emerging human lung tissue-based translational model precision cut lung slices (PCLS) highlights the need for advanced model systems in lung disease research. It explores recent advances in PCLS for studying infection and fibrosis, the use of ex vivo models to measure tissue function and understand COPD, and the application of PCLS for studying aging-related hallmarks and identifying biomarkers for premature lung aging. The adaptation of PCLS to incorporate cyclical stretching and the use of mathematical modeling for predicting antifibrotic therapeutic targets will also be discussed, alongside future challenges and perspectives in human PCLS use for drug development and validation.

Session Name: PG18 AI IN MEDICINE: EDUCATING THE FUTURE, TRANSFORMING PRACTICE
Description: This dynamic session explores strategies for medical educators navigating the evolving landscape of AI in education. Focusing on preclerkship and clerkship learning, assessment practices, and faculty development, it addresses the ethical, valid, and unbiased integration of AI tools. Participants will examine the opportunities and challenges AI presents in enhancing learning while guarding against cognitive deskilling. Through case-based discussion and practical frameworks, the session offers guidance on fostering adaptive expertise, ensuring assessment integrity, and promoting critical engagement with technology. Educators will leave equipped to thoughtfully harness AI’s potential while preserving core clinical reasoning and judgment in medical training.

Session Name: Respiratory Society of Americas Session: Interstitial Lung Disease Across the Americas: Adult and Pediatric Perspectives
Description:
This collaborative session, organized by the American Thoracic Society (ATS) in partnership with the American College od Chest Physicians (CHEST), the Canadian Thoracic Society (CTS), the Latin American Thoracic Association (ALAT), and the Brazilian Thoracic Society (SBPT), will examine how interstitial lung disease (ILD) is diagnosed and managed across the Americas, alternating between pediatric and adult perspectives. Speakers representing each society will highlight regional differences in clinical practice, access to diagnostic tools and therapies, and health system challenges, while identifying shared gaps and opportunities for cross-society collaboration. The symposium will conclude with a panel discussion focused on common themes, regional inequities, and next steps, including development of a joint perspective paper to advance ILD care across diverse settings.

Session Name: G1 Opening Ceremony
Description:
A nationally recognized leader in hospital medicine and health system innovation, Robert M. Wachter, MD, launches the ATS 2026 International Conference with a can’t-miss talk titled “How AI is Transforming Health Care” at the Opening Ceremony, from 4:15 to 5:30 p.m. on Saturday, May 16. Dr. Wachter will share timely insights from his new book, A Giant Leap: How AI is Transforming Healthcare and What That Means for Our Future, which examines how AI is already entering hospitals and clinics to impact patient care. While unflinchingly confronting the risks of AI, Dr. Wachter also explores opportunities for AI to match, and even surpass, human physicians in areas ranging from diagnosis to empathy. 

Dr. Wachter is professor and chair of the Department of Medicine at the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF). The author of more than 300 articles and six books, he coined the term “hospitalist” and is a past president of the Society of Hospital Medicine, past chair of the American Board of Internal Medicine, and an elected member of the National Academy of Medicine. The Opening Ceremony is free for all registered attendees of the International Conference, offering an early opportunity to connect with peers and hear from some of medicine’s most prominent thought leaders. 

This year, the Opening Ceremony will recognize the following Respiratory Health Award recipients: 
- Public Service Award: Tyra Bryant-Stephens, MD

- J. Randall Curtis Humanism Award: Lynn F. Reinke, PhD, ATSF 
- Edward Livingston Trudeau Medal: Charles G. Irvin, PhD, ATSF 
- J. Burns Amberson Lecture: Marc Peters-Golden, MD

Session Name: A2 VISUALIZING THE TARGET: IMAGE-BASED MULTIMODAL PROFILING OF MICRO AND MACROENVIRONMENT IN LUNG DISEASE
Description: A deeper molecular understanding of lung disease pathobiology is essential for developing targeted therapies and improving disease monitoring. Recent advances in spatial omics, and microscopic and molecular imaging methods have opened new frontiers in biomarker discovery and spatial characterization of lung disease initiation and development. This session will first outline clinical challenges and unmet needs, followed by highlighting cutting-edge multimodal approaches that are reshaping our understanding of pulmonary diseases, including spatial transcriptomics and proteomics, optical coherence tomography, and molecular PET imaging. Finally, it will focus on applying these tools in clinical trials, drawing insights from other disciplines (e.g.: oncology).

Session Name: A8 THE WOUNDED LUNG: CELLULAR STRESS, INFLAMMATION AND CARCINOGENESIS
Description: This symposium will explore how cellular stress and immune dysregulation contribute to the pathogenesis of lung injury and carcinogenesis. Experts in basic and translational research will highlight emerging mechanisms by which epithelial damage, chronic inflammation, and immune remodeling shape the injured lung microenvironment and drive malignant transformation. Emphasis will be placed on the intersection of stress signaling, host immunity, and epithelial plasticity as convergent pathways linking injury to cancer.

Session Name: A10 IS IT SARCOIDOSIS? - I DON'T KNOW
Description: The diagnosis of sarcoidosis can be challenging, often mimicking other granulomatous diseases and requiring careful exclusion of alternative etiologies. This session will provide a unique opportunity for clinicians to engage with leading experts on the diagnostic dilemmas encountered in sarcoidosis. The session will focus on distinguishing sarcoidosis from other conditions presenting with granulomas, leveraging cutting-edge molecular and spatial analysis techniques, and bridging the gap between basic research and clinical practice.

Session Name: A7 FROM EARLY DEVELOPMENT THROUGH AGING: SEX AND GENDER EFFECTS ON CARDIOPULMONARY DISEASE
Description: This session will explore how biologic sex and gender influence pulmonary vascular and right ventricular health from fetal life through aging. Speakers will examine hormonal, chromosomal, and lifestyle factors that drive remodeling of the pulmonary circulation and RV, affecting disease susceptibility, progression, and treatment response in pulmonary hypertension. Through life stages including fetal development, childhood through adolescence, pregnancy, loss of gonadal function, and aging, the symposium will present integrated basic, translational, and clinical perspectives. The session will conclude by addressing sex-based disparities in treatment decisions and drug development, offering a roadmap toward individualized therapies in pulmonary vascular disease.

Session Name: A12 DO NO HARM, UNLESS THE AI SAYS OTHERWISE - AI ETHICS, A PRO/CON
Description: AI tools are being implemented at a dizzying pace, yet the decision-making processes of these tools are not necessarily bound to the personal, societal, and professional ethics of human healthcare providers and researchers. This creates questions we must answer including who is responsible when AI recommendations cause harm, when and how do we tell patients that AI was involved in their care, how should clinical ethics committees and IRBs evaluate bias in AI tools, and how are ethical principles integrated in learning algorithms. This session will feature a series of pro/con discussions addressing these questions and others.

Session Name: A11 ADVANCING HEALTHCARE QUALITY THROUGH WORKFORCE EQUITY
Description: The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) identifies six dimensions of healthcare quality: safety, efficacy, timeliness, efficiency, patient-centeredness, and equity. Yet equity remains underemphasized despite persistent disparities in outcomes. Recent U.S. policy shifts further challenge traditional strategies, creating urgency for innovative, actionable approaches. This symposium presents evidence-based strategies to embed equity into workforce development and institutional quality improvement. Sessions move from a big-picture view of equity in healthcare quality to targeted approaches in evaluation, mentorship, and data analytics, concluding with concrete steps to build an inclusive, high-performing workforce delivering consistently high-quality, equitable care across settings.

Session Name: A9 PRIMARY CILIARY DYSKINESIA IN A GENOMIC THERAPEUTIC ERA
Description: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is a multimorbid inherited lung condition. Symptoms include neonatal respiratory distress, oto-sino- pulmonary disease and recurrent infections leading to bronchiectasis in adults. It is significantly underdiagnosed. Advances in genomic medicine pave the way for neonatal diagnosis and genetic therapies. This session will cover state of the art in diagnosis and treatment with a focus on improving health disparities in genetic diseases to improve equity, and inclusion. The session will highlight the first joint ATS/ERS diagnostic guideline (to be published end 2025), the completion of the 4 year NIH clingen gene project defining disease - gene associations, patient priorities and access in low resource settings and the latest in therapeutic trials.

Session Name: A4 HOST-DIRECTED THERAPEUTICS IN SEPSIS: LESSONS LEARNED AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
Description: Sepsis, defined as a dysregulated host response to infection, remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Yet treatment largely focuses on antibiotics and source control, with limited strategies to modulate the host response. Identifying pathways to recalibrate immune responses has emerged as a priority for NHLBI and ATS. The success of host-directed therapies (HDTs) in COVID-19—such as dexamethasone and tocilizumab—has reinvigorated interest in HDTs for sepsis. This symposium will feature international leaders discussing the current HDT landscape, key lessons from past trials, and how ongoing studies aim to advance precision immunomodulation in sepsis.

Session Name: A6 THE OBESE LUNG MICROENVIRONMENT: NEW INSIGHTS INTO ASTHMA PATHWAYS AND THERAPEUTIC TARGETS

This symposium will explore multifaceted mechanisms that link metabolic dysregulation within cells or in the context of metabolic disease. to airway inflammation, smooth muscle function, neural regulation, and immune responses. We aim to bring together investigators across disciplines— from molecular and cellular biology to systems biology, translational science and clinical research. This session will highlight emerging basic and translational research—from smooth muscle remodeling, neuro-immune-endocrine interactions, and emerging omics approaches that offer insight into disease heterogeneity and potential therapeutic targets.

Session Name: Roadmap to Clean Air and Healthier Lungs
Description:
Ambient, household and workplace air pollution are a leading contributor to respiratory morbidity and mortality, causing or exacerbating conditions such as asthma, COPD, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections. The global burden is substantial, with over 8 million deaths annually, and the effects are especially pronounced in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and among vulnerable populations. LMICs incur a higher proportion of disability-adjusted life years lost as a result of noncommunicable diseases attributable to air pollution and over 90% of air pollution-related deaths. In most LMICs, this disease and mortality burden has increased significantly over recent decades as a result of increased levels of pollution along with a growing and ageing population.

Session Name: NSC2 Conducting High-Impact Pulmonary Research in Low-and Middle-Income Countries
Description: Research in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) faces barriers including limited funding, infrastructure gaps, and reduced access to advanced technologies. Yet these regions carry a disproportionate burden of respiratory diseases, providing unique opportunities for impactful and globally relevant science. This session will bring together investigators with experience leading projects in LMICs to explore strategies for designing research that is feasible, sustainable, and innovative in resource-limited settings. Panelists will highlight lessons learned from studies on interstitial lung diseases, tuberculosis, air pollution, and COVID-19. Discussion will emphasize practical tools to establish equitable international collaborations, ensure fair authorship and data sharing, and leverage digital platforms to overcome logistical barriers. The interactive format will engage participants in small-group exchanges and open Q&A, encouraging early-career attendees to contribute ideas and explore partnerships. Ultimately, this session will demonstrate how LMIC-based research can inform guidelines, shape policy, and improve respiratory health globally.

Session Name: MTE10 USE OF BIOLOGIC THERAPIES IN THE TREATMENT OF INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE
Description: Treatment strategy for patients with interstitial lung disease due to underlying connective tissue disease (CTD-ILD) is nuanced, with clinical practice patterns evolving ahead of robust data and oftentimes requiring individualized decisions based on patient-specific factors. Attendees will gain insights into the rationale for biologic use, current evidence supporting their efficacy and safety, and considerations for clinical decision-making in the treatment of ILD. Real-world cases will illustrate how multidisciplinary approaches can optimize outcomes. Learners will be equipped with practical strategies for initiating and monitoring biologic treatments to best navigate the evolving therapeutic landscape.

Session Name: MTE13 MICROPLASTICS: RESEARCH CHALLENGES, OPPORTUNITIES, AND APPROACHES
Description: The session will provide insights into studying emerging inhalation toxicants, microplastics, with an expert in the field, Dr. Rebecca Florsheim. Dr. Florsheim will share findings from recent research about the accumulation of microplastics in human tissues, as well as rising concerns about weathered microplastic and their potential implication to human health including the respiratory system. Session Name: MTE2 A PRACTICAL GUIDE TO USING GENERATIVE AI IN RESEARCH
Description: Artificial intelligence is transforming the way we conduct research, introducing novel methodologies and improving efficiency across the research process. In this session, we will discuss how to implement generative AI in pulmonary and critical care research. We will examine use cases where generative AI excels, as well as situations where it may not be the appropriate tool. We will also discuss how to use generative AI with confidential data safely. Session Name: ME101 COMMUNICATING AND TEACHING ABOUT UNCERTAINTY IN CLINICAL, EDUCATION, AND RESEARCH SETTINGS
Description: Uncertainty is rampant in medicine following the pandemic and in the current socio-political environment where everything from Medicaid to NIH funding changes daily. In this interactive session, learners will be able to define uncertainty and distinguish it from confidence, review literature on its relevance to critical care, learn strategies used by other professions who deal routinely with uncertainty (e.g. engineers, meteorologists, military, and public health experts), and employ techniques on how to manage uncertainty. Session Name: MTE5 BRONCHIECTASIS: A SILENT STORM BEHIND THE COUGH
Description: Bronchiectasis is a condition with rising global incidence and prevalence. The diagnosis and management of bronchiectasis can be challenging given its heterogeneous etiologies with limited treatment options apart from airway clearance therapies. Bronchiectasis exacerbations are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality. Newer treatments aim to target various chronic airway infections and airway inflammation. This session will bridge knowledge gaps in managing complex patients with chronic cough from bronchiectasis and addressing targeted treatment modalities towards the 'vicious vortex' leading to progression of disease. Session Name: MTE7 EXPLORING PUBLIC DATASETS AND INTEGRATING MULTI-OMICS FOR TRANSLATIONAL RESEARCH: AN INVESTIGATOR'S GUIDE TO NAVIGATING THE WORLD OF OMICS
Description: With the rapid expansion of publicly available single-cell and multi-omics datasets, the potential for high-impact research in pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine is greater than ever. This session aims to empower researchers, especially early-career investigators to harness publicly available datasets and resources for hypothesis generation, data-driven discovery, and translational insight. By showcasing accessible tools, key repositories, and examples of successful data reuse, we will demystify the process of integrating large-scale omics data into individual research pipelines. Through a mix of case studies, tool walkthroughs, and a live demonstration, participants will walk away with actionable strategies for translating public omics data into meaningful discoveries.

Session Name: MTE6 THE MULTIFACETED ROLE OF FLEXIBLE BRONCHOSCOPY IN CHILDHOOD ASTHMA: FROM DIAGNOSIS TO PHENOTYPING AND PRECISION CARE
Description: Severe uncontrolled asthma (SUA) is defined as an inability to achieve asthma control despite aggressive management with high dose inhaled corticosteroid and another controller. Flexible bronchoscopy allows for characterization of lower airway inflammation and assessment of comorbidities including airway abnormalities and infection. Esophagoscopy may be done in conjunction with bronchoscopy to rule out eosinophilic esophagitis, which is another comorbidity of SUA. The session will outline the role of flexible bronchoscopy in pediatric SUA with special attention to endoscopic techniques and interpretation of the results of airway sampling as well as creation of personalized management plans

Session Name: Towards a Global Framework for Lung Health – The Forum of International Respiratory Societies (FIRS) Lung Health Taskforce
Description:
The Forum of International Respiratory Societies (FIRS) Lung Health Taskforce is an initiative aimed at improving how lung health is conceptualised, assessed, and discussed globally. In partnership with the Global Lung Function Initiative (GLI), the Taskforce brings together experts to lay the groundwork for a global standard in considering lung health. To date, the Taskforce has developed a Spirometry Toolkit, including a Global Spirometry Standard Operating Procedure and Training Framework, and has identified key biological, environmental, and social factors influencing lung health across the life course. Building on this work, the Taskforce is exploring the principles and pathways that could inform the future development of a Global Lung Health Index in the context of the growing global burden of respiratory disease. This session introduces the Taskforce’s work, highlights current areas of consensus, and outlines emerging directions for how lung health might be measured and compared globally in the future.

Session Name: NSC3 Advocacy Roadmap: A Path to Career and Advocacy Integration
Description: Advocacy is an integral part of the medical education framework. The American Board of Internal Medicine and the American Board of Pediatrics call for an understanding and duty to advocate in their statements of professionalism. The Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) Pediatrics Residency Review Committee requires advocacy training and experience for pediatric residents. Advocacy in healthcare and health policy arenas is often viewed more broadly as an opportunity for interprofessional collaboration. Nurses are one of the most trusted professionals in health care, are usually considered natural advocates at the bedside, and nursing organizations such as the American Nurses Association are increasingly calling for nurses to become advocates on the community, state, and national level. Scientific organizations such as the National Science Foundation, Nature Publishing Group and the American Association for the Advancement of Science encourage members to engage in scientific advocacy and describe it as a scientific imperative. Effective advocacy strategies include collaborating with key stakeholders, legislators, and professional organizations while extending to state, national, and international levels. However, there is a gap in mentoring early career professionals in integrating strategic advocacy efforts into their career goals. Knowing the importance of advocacy and recognizing how to advocate effectively are critical to the development of both clinical healthcare providers and researchers at all career levels. This session is formulated to encourage early career members to find accessible ways to advocate using their expert skills.

Session Name: ATS Diversity Forum
Description:
The annual ATS Diversity Forum celebrates diversity within the fields of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine and research.The Diversity Forum is an inclusive event, and we encourage all ATS members and International Conference attendees who are able to join us. The event is designed to provide accessible career insights and networking opportunities in a welcoming environment. 

This year’s theme is “Resilience in a Time of Challenge.” We are thrilled to welcome our featured speaker, Jennifer L. Taylor, MD, MSCS, ATSF, who will bring this theme to life in a truly impactful way. 

Dr. Taylor is a tenured professor of adult and pediatric pulmonary medicine at National Jewish Health (NJH), where she serves as Medical Director of Clinical Research Services, co-director of the Adult Cystic Fibrosis (CF) Program, and Director of the CF Therapeutics Development Network center. After receiving her undergraduate degree in human biology from Stanford University, she went on to receive her MD, combined internal medicine/pediatrics residency, and pulmonary Fellowship at Duke University, as well as a Master of Clinical Science from the University of Colorado. A leader in clinical trial design and conduct, she has served as national and global primary investigator on numerous CF pharmaceutical trials and co-leads the 41-site MAYFLOWERS study on maternal and fetal outcomes in the era of modulators. Her research also explores respiratory disease in orangutans, and she has authored over 160 manuscripts, a book, and multiple chapters. She holds editorial roles with the Journal of Cystic Fibrosis and Lancet Respiratory Medicine and chairs the American Thoracic Society International Conference Committee (2025–2027). 

Beyond research, Dr. Taylor is a strong advocate for racial justice and health equity in CF care. She co-founded NJH’s Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion council and served as interim Associate Vice President of DEI. Nationally, she has contributed to initiatives such as the CFF Racial Justice Working Group, ATS workshops on systemic racism in pediatric asthma, and NIH advisory efforts focused on equity in CF research. She collaborates with patient organizations to raise awareness of CF in people of color. Her achievements have earned her election to the American Society for Clinical Investigation and numerous honors, including the ATS Distinguished Achievement Award (2023), Emily’s Entourage CF Trailblazer Award (2022), and Cystic Fibrosis Research Incorporated CF Champion Award (2021). 

We also honor the recipients of the Underrepresented Trainee Development Scholarships (UTDS). These scholarships are designed to help increase diversity among underrepresented trainees in medicine by sponsoring attendance at the ATS International Conference. Recipients are selected based on the quality of the science presented in their submitted abstracts, along with other criteria. 

ATS thanks Genentech for their generous support of the Diversity Forum.

Session Name: NSC4 Navigating Prior Authorization Challenges and Finding Solutions
Description: While implemented with the stated goal of improving the efficiency and cost of clinical care, prior authorization (PA) denials by third-party payers have led to serious, unintended yet predictable consequences. The American Medical Association (AMA) found that 91% of physicians reported that patients experience delays in needed care and worse clinical outcomes, and that 75% of patients abandoned needed treatment due to burdens associated with the PA process. A meta-analysis (Murphy, Am J Med, 2025) of 25 studies in oncology, cardiology, behavioral health and pediatrics found that PA burden led to harm including delayed care, disease progression or exacerbation, preventable hospitalization, and prolonged hospital stay, with lower rates of disease-free survival. The AMA also found that the PA process exacerbates clinician burnout. The use of artificial intelligence by some payers in the PA process has added to clinicians’ frustration in addressing denials for necessary care. A systematic exploration of the impact of PA denials in pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine, however, has not been done. We propose an interactive panel discussion, including bidirectional engagement facilitated by the audience response system, to explore the impact of PA denials on patients and ATS members in pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine, in pediatric and adult populations. The session is open to clinicians, educators, administrators, and interested researchers. Speakers in pulmonary, critical care and sleep medicine will provide background information, present illustrative cases, generate audience response, and review potential avenues to move forward on behalf of our patients and their clinician advocates.

Session Name: One Scan, Two Functions: Bringing Non-Contrast Ventilation–Perfusion Mapping into Everyday CT Practice
Description:
Pulmonary disease is fundamentally functionaldefined by abnormalities in ventilation and perfusionyet most routine imaging available to pulmonologists remains purely structural. CT:VQ bridges that gap by generating ventilation and perfusion maps directly from standard noncontrast inspiratory/expiratory chest CT scans, allowing clinicians to visualize regional lung function with the anatomical clarity of CT.

Fully FDAcleared and compatible with any vendor's CT scanner, CT:VQ integrates seamlessly into existing workflows as an automated postprocessing layer. There are no contrast injections, no radiotracers, no additional scanner time, and no new acquisition protocols. Results appear in PACS as colorcoded functional maps, quantitative lobar metrics, V/Q mismatch visualizations, and a structured report that can prepopulate pulmonology or radiology reporting templates.

For pulmonologists managing PE, CTEPH, COPD, asthma, ILD, bronchiectasis, preoperative lung resection, or lung volume reduction candidates, CT:VQ offers precise regional functional assessment that can improve risk stratification, identify heterogeneous ventilation defects, clarify perfusion deficits, and reveal regional functional deterioration that may precede structural changes.

By leveraging a scan already central to pulmonary care, CT:VQ expands access to functional lung imagingespecially in centers without nuclear V/Q capability or for patients unable to tolerate contrast or radiopharmaceuticalswhile supporting more confident clinical decisionmaking with comprehensive functional intelligence derived from a single CT scan.

Description: Complex in vitro models (CIVMs), when used as part of new approach methodologies, are transforming pulmonary research, yet variability in culture systems continues to limit experimental reproducibility. PneumaCult cell culture media addresses this challenge by providing a standardized, high-performance workflow for the efficient expansion and differentiation of human bronchial, small airway, and nasal epithelial cells. By generating physiologically relevant, fully differentiated lung epithelia, these CIVMs enable consistent and reliable results across applications. From respiratory disease modeling and drug discovery to toxicity testing and epithelial biology, PneumaCult helps bridge the gap between in vitro systems and translational insight.
Speakers/Roles: Kramer, Philipp (Speaker)

Session Name: NSC5 Strategies for Success in Leadership
Description: This session is sponsored by the Pediatric Pulmonology Division Directors Association (PPDDA) Executive Leadership Team. Many physicians lack confidence in pursuing or starting new leadership roles within or outside of their home institution. Though some of us receive formal training on how to be effective leaders, many are elected to these roles without knowledge or experience advocating for system change and resources. Leadership skills are often learned “real time” or from challenging situations but rarely do new directorships or leadership roles come with formal onboarding or a timeline for mastery of defined skillsets. Asking for specific job descriptions, a list of institutional allies and mentors along with a specific “checklist” for leadership onboarding could make a significant impact on job satisfaction for new leaders and retention of talent in these roles. There should also be transparency about the relevant organizational structure in academic medicine and how to best align with teams to advocate effectively. This would benefit all trainees and faculty and would help with effective project and program proposals. Through the use of a moderated panel discussion with current national leaders this session aims to: (1) Define the challenges of entering a new leadership role (2) Highlight opportunities to establish “early wins” as new leaders advocate for their teams (3) Focus on the importance of mentorship and sponsorship in leadership roles, with a particular focus on women and underrepresented minorities; and (4) Encourage interest in pursuing leadership roles amongst trainees and junior faculty.
Location: Learning Studio, Hall C (Level II, OCCC West)

Session Name: Advancements in Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency (AATD): Aiming for AAT Restoration and  Clinically Meaningful Endpoints
Description:
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) remains a highly underdiagnosed condition, despite being the most
common genetic risk factor for COPD. This symposium will underscore the importance of proactive, early
AATD screening for timely intervention. We will then delve into the compelling evidence supporting the need
to restore AAT levels to their normal range, which requires novel therapeutic approaches. Finally, we will
identify clinical outcomes which may have the potential to address this need. Join us to gain crucial insights
into the evolving landscape of AATD, empowering you to optimize patient identification and management
while advocating for the next generation of effective therapies.

Session Name: Beyond the Airway: Conversations That Shape Severe Asthma Treatment Decisions
Description:
Through live clinician-patient dialogue, this session will explore real-world factors that shape treatment decision-making and long-term management in severe asthma. Despite advances in therapy, care is often influenced by challenges that extend beyond the airway, including clinical complexity, treatment burden, and patient preferences.

The conversation will focus on how practical considerations ranging from individual lifestyle demands and patient preferences to health disparities inform clinical decisions. Shared decision-making will be highlighted as a critical framework for meaningful, patient-centered conversations that align clinical objectives with what matters most to patients. By bringing clinician-patient perspectives to the forefront, this session aims to offer practical insights into optimizing severe asthma care through intentional, collaborative treatment discussions that support sustained asthma management.
Speakers/Roles: Lugogo, Njira L. (Speaker); Maselli, Diego J. (Speaker)

Session Name: Triple Therapy in Focus: Tailored Approaches to Obstructive Lung Disease
Description: Recent evidence is reshaping the role of a triple therapy option in respiratory care. In this session, Cedric "Jamie" Rutland, MD, and Joseph Khabbaza, MD, discuss clinical findings and offer patient-centric insight on how the evidence aligns with current considerations in disease management.

Session Name: ATS LGBTQIA+ Interest Group Meeting
Description:
***Attendance is limited*** 

This is the official business meeting for the ATS LGBTQIA+ Interest Group. 

The ATS LGBTQIA+ Interest Group provides resources and strives to foster an inclusive, equitable, and supportive environment for LGBTQIA+ individuals and allies within the respiratory, sleep, and critical care fields. Our mission is to promote health equity, advance research, and improve health care access and outcomes for LGBTQIA+ patients by addressing unique health disparities and supporting our workforce. We are committed to educating health care professionals, advocating for policy changes, and championing the voices of LGBTQIA+ individuals in our society. Through collaboration, mentorship, and community engagement, we work to create an environment that values diversity, respects identities, and empowers all individuals to thrive.

Session Name: FeNO in Practice: Current Applications and Emerging Opportunities
Description:
Fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) has become an increasingly valuable tool in the diagnosis and management of airway inflammation, particularly in asthma care. In this session, Carol Stonham MBE will explore how FeNO is currently being applied in clinical practice, including its role in diagnosis, treatment monitoring, and guiding personalised therapy decisions.

The presentation will also highlight emerging opportunities for FeNO use, with a forward-looking perspective on evolving applications such as asthmaCOPD overlap and other complex respiratory conditions. Attendees will gain practical insights into integrating FeNO into routine workflows, as well as expert perspectives on where the field is heading.

Designed for clinicians and healthcare professionals seeking to optimise patient outcomes, this session will provide both a solid foundation in current use and a glimpse into the future potential of FeNO in respiratory care.
Categories (all): Asthma

Session Name: The Duality of IL-33 in COPD: Inflammation and Mucus Dysfunction
Description:
Is there more than one way to think about IL-33 in COPD?
Inflammation, epithelial damage, and mucus dysfunction are central features of COPD. IL-33 is a
cytokine expressed in the lung and is released in response to epithelial injury. Two bioactive forms of
IL-33 have been described, a reduced form (IL-33RED) and an oxidized form (IL-33OX), which play
distinct roles in driving inflammatory pathways and mucus dysfunction in COPD, respectively.
Join a leading expert to explore IL-33 dual pathways may contribute to the
pathogenesis of COPD. Discover the duality of IL-33 in COPD.
Speakers/Roles: Kraft, Monica (Speaker)
Categories (all): COPD

Session Name: NSC6 Resources From the NIGMS Sepsis Human Biospecimens Program
Description: NIGMS intends to achieve maximal sharing and utilization of the biospecimens, datasets, and methods among interested investigators. The NIGMS Human Sepsis Biospecimens program initiative under PAR-21-077 is now in its late phase and has evaluated human samples and data collected from the 7 funded R21 projects and 9 R33 projects, with a wide range of patient cohorts (from neonates to adults) and sample types (such as dried whole bloods, PBMCs, HME filters). Additionally, the awards have supported new methods development for efficient collection and preservation of biospecimens (e.g., Cryo-preservation of whole blood and Redox trapping for biospecimens) and for biospecimen analysis (single cell transcriptome and integrated multiomics for phenotyping). In support of the goals of the program to share clinical materials and analytical methods with the broader research community, and to enable future research with sepsis and critically ill patient-derived specimens, investigators have agreed to share the results of their work. They will discuss their collections and potential future collaborations, as well as their ideas, data, methods, and best practices for biorepository creation and use. Come to this network event to be part of the timely discussion and be at the forefront of NIH priority to prioritize human-based research technologies.

Session Name: A84 PRISM, GOLD 0, AND PRE-COPD: USEFUL CONCEPTS OR DIAGNOSTIC OVERREACH?

Session Name: A87 YOU BREATHE WHAT YOU EAT - EFFECTS OF NUTRITION ON LUNG HEALTH AND DISEASE
Description: Modern lifestyles have led to rising obesity rates, now a major global health concern linked to chronic diseases, including respiratory conditions. Nutrition plays a dual role: while high-calorie diets and maternal obesity contribute to lung disease, specific nutrients (e.g., DHA, vitamin E, retinoic acid) may support lung development and immune function. Emerging evidence highlights complex interactions between diet, obesity, and the pulmonary microenvironment across the lifespan. Session Name: NSC7 Physician Wellbeing 2.0 (Beyond the Warm and Fuzzy Hour)
Description: Traditionally, the burden of maintaining well-being has been placed on the individual physician, with solutions focused on yoga, meditation, mindfulness, or resilience training. While these approaches have value, they often fail to address the structural and cultural drivers of burnout. As one wellness leader aptly stated, “you cannot meditate away a toxic work environment.” This session, Physician Wellbeing 2.0 (Beyond the Warm and Fuzzy Hour), will explore the evolution of physician wellness, emphasizing the urgent need to move from individual-focused strategies toward system-level and institutional interventions. Landmark studies will be discussed that tie physician wellbeing with improvement in workplace efficiency and supportive organizational cultures. Participants will engage with the evidence base, understand the business case for investing in physician wellbeing, and learn proven strategies that institutions can adopt to reduce burnout and enhance professional fulfillment. By equipping attendees with tools to advocate for systemic change, we aim to shift the narrative from “self-care as survival” to activism for an institutional commitment to thriving careers. OBJECTIVES 1. Describe the evolution of physician wellness paradigms from individual-focused strategies to system-level and institutional interventions. (Participants will be able to articulate key shifts in the conceptual framework of physician wellbeing, supported by landmark literature), including making the business-case for physician wellbeing). 2. Identify systemic and institutional contributors to physician burnout and evaluate evidence-based interventions aimed at improving workplace culture and efficiency. (Participants will examine data-driven approaches to wellness, moving beyond personal resilience to strategies embedded in organizational structure).

Description:
Everyone has a story to tell. Join us at the Networking Super Center, SpeakEasy, on select days and times to hear how successful ATS members navigated and overcame significant hurdles in their careers. 

Sushma Cribbs, MD, MSc, ATSF 

Dr. Cribbs is a Professor of Medicine in the Division of Pulmonary, Allergy, Critical Care & Sleep Medicine at Emory University. She received her undergraduate and medical degree from Boston University and then completed her Internal Medicine residency, Pulmonary/Critical Care fellowship, and a Master of Science in Clinical Research from Emory University. Dr. Cribbs joined the faculty in 2009 and has held several leadership roles including Medical Director of the Pulmonary Clinic at Grady Memorial Hospital, Associate Program Director of the Pulmonary & Critical Care Fellowship Program, and Director of the Home Oxygen Respiratory Program at the Atlanta VA Hospital. 

Dr. Cribbs is currently the Vice Chair for Faculty Development in the Department of Medicine, where she is responsible for the creation and oversight of innovative faculty development programming (including workshops, conferences, mentoring and distinction programs) and leads the department’s promotions and tenure process for all 950+ faculty. Dr. Cribbs’ has also taken her dedication and passion for career development to her national professional society, the American Thoracic Society (ATS), where she has been instrumental in developing, organizing, and implementing novel career development and educational bootcamps, workshops, and training programs for early career members of ATS including the Center for Career Development, the Faculty Development Series, the Student Scholars Program and ATS’s New Faculty Boot Camp at the ATS International Conference. For her dedication and hard work, she received the ATS Presidential Commendation in 2022. 

Dr. Cribbs has also made significant contributions to the field of Pulmonary & Critical Care Medicine centered around her passions for career development, education, and her scientific interests in HIV-related lung disease, which have now expanded to COVID-19. She has led several multi-disciplinary translational research projects to elucidate the mechanisms by which HIV and other infectious insults affect lung immunity, rendering individuals susceptible to lung infections and lung injury. She is currently leading the NIH “RECOVER study: A Multi-site Observational Study of Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 Infection in Adults” at the Atlanta VA, which will further our understanding of the long-term impact of COVID-19 in adults. She is currently based at the Atlanta VA where she sees patients and supervises medical students, residents, and fellows.

Session Name: Gaining Control of Eosinophilic Disorders: Best Practices for Hypereosinophilic Syndrome and Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis
Description:
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) and hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) are both rare types of eosinophilic disorders. Diagnosis and management of these disorders is challenging due to their complex and overlapping pathologic features and heterogeneous systemic involvement. Both disorders carry substantial risks of morbidity and mortality due to delayed diagnosis and inadequate treatment. Interleukin (IL)-5 is a key driver of pathophysiology; therapies targeting IL-5 or the IL-5 receptor are a mainstay of treatment. 

In this confidence-based clinical decision CALIBRATE symposium, Drs. Praveen Akuthota, Philip Seo, and Michael Wechsler will discuss EGPA and HES patient cases with real-world, point-of-care decision checkpoints paired with confidence ratings to improve diagnosis and treatment sequencing.

This program brings together multidisciplinary perspectives from pulmonology, allergy and immunology, and otorhinolaryngology to explore shared underlying disease mechanisms in asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The engaging faculty panel will guide participants through an examination of epithelial cytokine signaling in airway diseases and practical therapeutic decision-making involving new and emerging biologic therapies that target these shared upstream mechanisms. Attendees will also learn about the latest clinical evidence for newer and emerging biologic therapies that target upstream epithelial cytokine signaling and discuss how to incorporate these novel therapies into mechanism-based treatment strategies, with an emphasis on optimizing disease control, reducing oral corticosteroid use, and improving outcomes across the unified airway. Session Name: Turning Down the Inflammatory Signal in COPD: Advancing Care With Biologic Therapies Targeting Upstream Cytokines
Description:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) encompasses a group of progressive and inflammatory lung diseases characterized by persistent respiratory symptoms and exacerbations resulting in decreased quality of life (QOL), hospitalization, irreversible lung damage, and progressively declining lung function. Conventional COPD treatment includes inhaled long-acting bronchodilators and steroids, but many patients continue to experience poor symptom control and frequent exacerbations.


Therapeutic advancements have significantly transformed COPD care, with biologicsinitially developed for type 2 inflammatory diseases like asthmanow being repurposed to target these shared type 2 inflammatory pathways in COPD. However, currently approved biologic therapy in COPD only targets eosinophilic inflammation, which accounts for a small subpopulation of patients with COPD. Fortunately, groundbreaking advances identified an upstream targetST2/IL33potentially impacting both eosinophilic and neutrophilic inflammation in COPD; this will provide opportunities for personalizing treatment and overcoming limitations of current therapies in a broader patient population (eg, patients with low eosinophils).


With the goal of helping clinicians adapt their practice in alignment with the growing role of biologics in the COPD treatment armamentarium, PeerView has prepared this Peer Pressure educational symposium. Our panel will discuss the latest data on integrating targeted biologics into updated treatment protocols and recent evidence on emerging options, factoring in safety, patient preferences, and QOL for patients with COPD. In this lively format, the experts will be put on the spot with clinical questions that spark spirited discussion, reveal key insights, and offer real-world guidance. Session Name: Bridging Lived and Clinical Experiences: Patient and Pulmonologist Perspectives in IPF and PPF
Description:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) are progressive, life-limiting interstitial lung diseases that present significant challenges for patients and clinicians that are marked by diagnostic delays, complex management, and persistent unmet needs. 
This symposium sponsored by Bristol Myers Squibb brings together a patient and a pulmonologist to offer complementary perspectives on the realities of living with and managing these diseases, linking these perspectives to the pathophysiology of IPF and PPF by exploring the underlying biology and signaling pathways.
An interactive dialogue between a pulmonologist and a patient will kick off the symposium by tracing the full IPF/PPF journey from early symptom onset and diagnostic hurdles to management approaches, highlighting the barriers patients face and the gaps that continue to affect outcomes and quality of life. 
The discussion then dives deeper into disease pathophysiology, exploring signaling pathways implicated in the three drivers of fibrogenesis (epithelial cell injury, inflammation/vascular leakage, and fibroblast expansion), and how the LPA-LPA1 pathway acts as a central mediator that mechanistically links these processes involved in IPF and PPF.
Join us as we bridge patient and clinical experience with expert-led insights into the biology of IPF and PPF and explore how our evolving understanding of pathophysiology may shape the future of care.

Session Name: Feuding With Fibrosing ILD: Pathways to Timely Diagnosis and Care
Description: Fibrosing interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) are progressive lung disorders associated with lung function decline, decreased quality of life, and increased mortality. Early, accurate identification is challenging but crucial, as delays often result in advanced disease and poorer outcomes. Traditional immunosuppressive therapies offer limited benefit, but novel agents targeting underlying fibrosis are reshaping management approaches. This Faculty Feud Symposium delivers a high-energy, interactive game-show experience that's as entertaining as it is educational! Expert faculty will present up-to-date insights on recognition, diagnosis, and evolving multidisciplinary strategies for managing fibrosing ILDsempowering clinicians with practical tools and current evidence. Join us to get up to speed on advances to improve patient care!

Session Name: NSC9 Getting Engaged in Clinical Trials: Pathways and Strategies for Budding Trialists
Description: Breaking in to clinical trials often appears daunting to early-career scientists, but there are many accessible and rewarding pathways to success as a trialist. This interactive session will demystify the varied pathways that budding trialists can pursue, offering practical strategies for getting involved and growing in the diverse world of pulmonary/critical care clinical trials. Through real-world examples, expert insights, and audience-driven discussion, participants will gain actionable tools to help navigate entry into the clinical trials ecosystem, contribute meaningfully to team trials and develop "starter" trials of their own, identify mentorship and collaboration opportunities, build knowledge and skills, and find funding tailored to early-career investigators. Mentors, educators, and institutional leaders will also gain insights into how to support and guide emerging trialists, foster inclusive research environments, and create opportunities for progressive engagement across disciplines. The session will emphasize inclusive pathways for diverse professionals—including physicians, RTs, pharmacists, nurses, and allied health researchers—highlighting how different backgrounds enrich clinical research. Attendees will leave with a clearer roadmap to becoming successful clinical trialists and contributing meaningfully to patient-centered research.

Session Name: B8 PULMONARY REHABILITATION IN NON-COPD PATIENTS: UPDATES ON THE EVIDENCE, CLINICAL INDICATIONS AND PHYSIOLOGY
Description: Pulmonary rehabilitation is an evidence-based intervention that improve symptoms, quality of life and exercise capacity in individuals with chronic lung disease. In non-COPD conditions, evidence for the benefits of pulmonary rehabilitation continues to evolve and will be highlighted through presentations on interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis and asthma. The presentation will go beyond the ATS 2023 PR guidelines that primarily focused on COPD, with less discussion of interstitial lung disease and pulmonary hypertension. It will include a patient speaker and a diverse group of chairs and speakers including clinicians, researchers, physiotherapists, early career professionals and senior professionals.

Session Name: B9 PULMONARY FUNCTION IN CHILDHOOD RESPIRATORY DISEASE: EVIDENCE, SOCIAL DETERMINANTS, AND TRAJECTORIES
Description: Pulmonary function testing (PFT) in children offers critical insight into pediatric respiratory disease, yet questions remain about its predictability. This session highlights the evolving role of spirometry, lung clearance index, oscillometry, and cardiopulmonary exercise testing across a spectrum of childhood respiratory diseases. Speakers will address the latest evidence linking PFTs to outcomes, and highlight knowledge in asthma, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, and primary ciliary dyskinesia. A cross-cutting theme will examine the impact of social determinants on lung function, and a final talk will examine childhood lung function trajectories into adulthood, highlighting the lifelong implications of pediatric respiratory health.

Session Name: B5 NOVEL INSIGHTS INTO THE COMPLEMENT INFLUENCE ON LUNG MICROENVIRONMENT IN ACUTE AND CHRONIC DISEASE
Description: Complement is considered a hepatic protein that operates in circulation. However, studies demonstrate complement is produced in the lung by respiratory epithelia, immune cells, and fibroblasts and is important for regulation of pulmonary immunity, tissue repair, and endothelial function. However critical gaps in our understanding for what happens when this multifunctional system becomes dysregulated during lung injury and fibrosis remain. This session explores mechanisms of complement promotion of ARDS, IPF, and PAH, and how lung transplant outcomes are influenced by increased levels. It will also address if genetic variants in complement regulation alter phenotypes in lung disease. Finally, we will discuss therapeutic interventions and the role of complement inhibition in lung disease.

Description: Climate change, environmental policy, and lung health intersect as respiratory illnesses intensify globally. Vulnerable populations—such as children, the elderly, historically marginalized, and socioeconomically disadvantaged communities—experience disproportionate exposure to air pollutants, heat, and allergens, compounding health inequities. In March 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) announced 31 actions to roll back various rules and programs protecting lung health from pollution. Environmental and Health Organizations, including the ATS, have released statements opposing these actions. This symposium will discuss the current environmental threats to lung health, including recent policy changes in the US and climate change globally, and provide tools to advocate and influence policy.

Session Name: B12 PRESIDENTS SYMPOSIUM: CELEBRATING SCIENCE: PULMONARY HYPERTENSION FROM BASIC DISCOVERIES, TO TRANSLATIONAL BREAKTHROUGHS, TO CLINICAL APPLICATIONS
Description:
Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is an example of a fatal disease transformed through mechanistic discovery into a treatable chronic condition. Over four decades, advances in vascular biology led to the identification of prostacyclin deficiency, endothelin overexpression, impaired nitric oxide signaling, and, most recently, dysregulated activin signaling—each translating into effective therapies that have reshaped patient outcomes. Despite these successes, many clinicians and trainees lack a cohesive understanding of how these discoveries were made, how they informed drug development, and how they should frame current and future therapeutic decisions. 

This Presidential Symposium brings together internationally recognized pioneers and leaders who were directly involved in the discovery, early translation, and clinical maturation of each major PAH therapeutic pathway. By tracing the scientific arc from initial observation through first-in-human studies and eventual clinical adoption, the session will clarify how translational science drives durable improvements in patient care. 

Attendees will gain a deeper mechanistic understanding of PAH therapies, improved ability to critically evaluate emerging treatments, and enhanced confidence in explaining treatment rationale to patients and trainees. Impact will be assessed through session evaluations measuring knowledge acquisition, relevance to clinical practice, and intent to incorporate mechanistic insights into patient care and research.

Session Name: NSC10 Elevator Speech Workshop: Sharpening Your Professional Identity
Description: Physician burnout remains pervasive, particularly among early-career professionals, and has driven many to leave medicine altogether. While multiple systemic and individual strategies to address burnout have been proposed, one underrecognized skill is learning how to set boundaries. Early in their careers, physicians are often encouraged—or feel compelled—to say “yes” to every invitation, project, or opportunity. While these commitments can foster growth, overcommitment frequently leads to exhaustion, loss of focus, and ultimately burnout. Cultivating the ability to discern when to say “yes” and when (and how) to say “no” is a vital, yet rarely taught, skill for long-term professional sustainability. This session will feature a panel of clinicians who will share their experiences, lessons learned, and practical strategies for boundary setting. Through a moderated discussion and interactive audience Q&A, participants will gain actionable insights into managing opportunities thoughtfully, setting limits, and reframing “no” as a positive step toward professional growth and well-being.

Session Name: The Underrecognized Burden of Asthma in Low and Middle-Income Countries
Description:
This session will raise awareness of the burden of asthma in LMICs, highlighting risk factors and approaches to management. Asthma in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remains a major yet underrecognized health burden. Limited access to diagnostic tools, underdiagnosis, inadequate treatment, and poor availability or affordability of essential medications, particularly inhaled corticosteroids, contribute to poor disease control. Many patients rely solely on short-acting β2-agonists, increasing the risk of severe exacerbations and death. National asthma plans and specialized care are uncommon, especially for children. Although asthma prevalence is generally lower than in high-income countries, symptom severity, rates of uncontrolled disease, and asthma-related deaths, particularly among women in low-SDI regions, are rising. Environmental exposures, comorbidities, and socioeconomic barriers further worsen outcomes, highlighting the urgent need to strengthen diagnosis, treatment access, and public health interventions in LMICs.

Session Name: MTE21 MANAGEMENT OF PULMONARY HYPERTENSION IN PATIENTS WITH OBESITY
Description:
The phenotypic profile of patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) has changed, due to a higher incidence of cardiopulmonary comorbidities in patients otherwise diagnosed as PAH. Among these comorbidities, obesity represents an important therapeutic challenge due to differences in physiology and clinical presentation. 
In this session, experts in PAH will discuss the changing epidemiology of PAH, with emphasis on severe obesity and cardiopulmonary comorbidities. We will review the physiology and diagnostic framework for this complex group of patients (advanced imaging, CPET, exercise catheterization). Finally, we will review the existing evidence related to therapeutic approaches for this particular syndrome.

We will discuss role of AI in modeling disease, including stratification and prediction. Lastly we will discuss how large language models have the potential to increase research efficiency and clinical trial enrollment. Session Name: MTE22 UNRAVELING THE STORM: MANAGING ACUTE EXACERBATIONS OF INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASES

Session Name: MTE15 POTENTIAL AND PITFALLS OF AI FOR CLINICIANS AND EDUCATORS

Session Name: Raising the Bar with SURPASS-IPF: The First Phase 3 Head-to-Head Superiority Trial in IPF Testing Deupirfenidone vs. Pirfenidone
Description:
A decade of challenges with first-generation antifibrotics has highlighted the need for better therapeutic options. Pulmonologists and people living with IPF state that enhanced efficacy is the number one enduring unmet need. While some novel IPF agents focus on improving tolerability, deupirfenidone is a new investigational IPF treatment that seeks to offer increased efficacy. 

In this session, we will introduce you to SURPASS-IPF: The first Phase 3 head-to-head trial in IPF powered to test for superiority of deupirfenidone over an approved antifibrotic, pirfenidone. Deupirfenidone is a strategically deuterated form of pirfenidone that retains established antifibrotic activity while offering a differentiated pharmacokinetic profile that may translate into enhanced efficacy with favorable tolerability. The SURPASS-IPF study design reflects a goal to improve upon the efficacy offered by standard of care for people living with this devastating disease, and represents a critical step forward in IPF drug development. 

Join our discussion with IPF expert Dr. Toby Maher at Innovation Hub 3 (booth 650), Monday, May 18th at 11:05 AM to learn more about deupirfenidone and Celea Therapeutics' Phase 3 SURPASS-IPF superiority trial vs. pirfenidone.

Session Name: From Insight to Intervention: Future Clinical Pathways Enabled by CT‑Based Non-Contrast Ventilation–Perfusion Pulmonary Mapping
Description:
This forward-looking session brings together leading clinicians to discuss how CT:VQ may transform future pulmonary care pathways by enabling functional ventilationperfusion assessment directly from routine non contrast CT. 
The session will include an overview of the technological developments led by the Prof. Andreas Fouras, CTO and CEO of 4DMedical. He will explain how these developments can support clinical workflows and invite clinical experts to discuss their impact in their respective areas of interest. 
Dr. Mehul Gilani will outline the evolving role of CT-derived perfusion and V/Q mismatch in PE and CTEPH management. Dr. Mike Lester will explore how regional ventilation and small airway heterogeneity mapping could shape the future of COPD phenotyping, disease monitoring, and outcomes prediction. He will also describe how functional CT may refine pneumothorax decision-making and collateral ventilation assessment, supporting more precise planning for interventions such as lung volume reduction therapy.
Together, these expert perspectives highlight how CT:VQ may streamline diagnostic pathways, enhance risk stratification, reduce reliance on nuclear medicine or any contrast-agents, and ultimately elevate the functional precision of pulmonary care across diverse clinical domains.

Session Name: SPS15 NAVIGATING HEALTH POLICY IN A CHANGING LANDSCAPE: COVERAGE, WORKFORCE, AND ADVOCACY
SPS16  FLORIDA AND ITS CRITICAL NEEDS
XTMAB-16 in Sarcoidosis: First-in-Patient Study Results
Description:
The Xentria team is pleased to invite you to join Dr. Ogugua N. Obi, Director of the ECU Sarcoidosis Center, as she presents the latest update on XTMAB-16 in Sarcoidosis: First-in-Patient Study Results. In this phase 1b/2a MAD study, XTMAB-16 demonstrated a favorable safety and tolerability profile in patients with pulmonary sarcoidosis, without unexpected TNF-inhibitor class effects. Preliminary efficacy signals suggest that XTMAB-16 may facilitate corticosteroid reduction while preserving lung function and improving patient-reported outcomes. These findings support continued clinical development and dose selection for further evaluation.

Sarcoidosis is a chronic, multisystem inflammatory disorder of unknown etiology that is characterized by the formation of granulomas in one or more organs in the body, with key pro-inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF) implicated in granuloma formation and disease persistence. Sarcoidosis affects people of all ages but most commonly affects young and middle-aged adults. There are fewer than 200,000 sarcoidosis patients in the US, and no therapies have been developed and approved specifically for the treatment of sarcoidosis to date. Chronic corticosteroid dependence and its associated complications continue to emphasize the unmet need for alternative treatment options for patients living with sarcoidosis. 

XTMAB-16 is a chimeric human-murine anti-TNF monoclonal antibody being developed as a biologic product for the treatment of pulmonary sarcoidosis with or without extra pulmonary involvement. Based on its ability to block TNF, XTMAB-16 may disrupt an inflammatory pathway and help slow granuloma formation. For more information on XTMAB-16, please visit xentria.com.

Session Name: Breaking the Cycle: Novel Airway Clearance Technologies and Their Role in Modern Bronchiectasis Care
Description:

This session will provide a focused review of the role of ACT across chronic respiratory conditions (including noncystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (NCFB) and cystic fibrosis), highlighting current evidence, real-world barriers, and gaps in comparative data across modalities.

The talk will introduce a practical framework for personalizing ACT based on patient characteristics, disease burden, and physiologic factors, moving beyond traditional step-up approaches. Emerging technologies, including novel airway clearance devices and techniques, will be discussed with an emphasis on their mechanisms of action, early clinical evidence, and potential role in expanding treatment options for patients who are not well served by conventional therapies.

Session Name: A Fresh Perspective on Inflammatory Diseases: Connecting Epithelial Cytokines in Severe Asthma, CRSwNP, and COPD
Description: Amgen & AstraZeneca invite you to explore a source of airway inflammation from a fresh perspective! Join us for an expert-led presentation where we will delve into the airway epithelium and the cytokines it can produce, which are actively being investigated as a source of severe asthma, chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP), COPD and beyond. Discover emerging data in epithelial-driven inflammatory disease and how the epithelium can serve as a critical link between inflammatory diseases.
Speakers/Roles: Moscolo, Maria (Speaker); Cardet, Juan Carlos (Speaker)
Categories (all): Asthma; COPD

Session Name: CyPath® Lung Testing in Practice
Description: The growing volume of pulmonary nodules driven by expanded screening and incidental findings is increasing clinical burden and complicating management. Providers need efficient, accurate tools to support decision-making. CyPath Lung is a noninvasive, cost-effective diagnostic test that uses flow cytometry and AI to analyze the lung microenvironment. Clinical data and case studies demonstrate its ability to detect cancer as early as Stage 1A, while a negative result can help avert unnecessary and often risky invasive procedures. With strong sensitivity and specificity, CyPath Lung supports clinical decision-making for both surveillance and intervention. The test is broadly applicable in high-risk patients, regardless of nodule size or prior cancer history.
Speakers/Roles: Downie, Gordon (Speaker)

Session Name: Unmet Needs in IPF Understanding Disease Burden and Current Approaches
Description: Explore the evolving landscape of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) in this engaging session, following the patient journey from early symptoms to diagnosis and disease burden. Gain key insights into IPF pathophysiology and epidemiology, while discussing unmet needs in management including treatment persistence, healthcare resource utilization, and discontinuation patterns associated with antifibrotic therapies.
Speakers/Roles: Maher, Toby (Speaker); Lee, Joyce (Speaker)

Session Name: 2026 BEAR Cage Competition
Description:
The top three submissions chosen in advance by the Drug/Device Discovery and Development (DDDD) committee will pitch their highly innovative research proposals to a panel of translational science experts representing academia, industry, and governmental sectors in front of a live audience at the ATS International Conference on Monday May 18, 2026 from 1:30-3:30PM EST located in the International Participants Center in the Orange County Convention Center.  

The panel, with audience participation, will "vet" these proposals with each presenter providing a unique "shark tank" like learning environment that fuels real-time feedback and propels the strategic thinking required for these novel ideas to become innovations. After each presentation, the live panel and audience will have sufficient time to ask questions to each of the top three contestants. Ultimately, the panel will award one grand prize winner a $10,000 prize and the two-runner proposals will receive $2,500 each.

Session Name: From concept to completion: A dialogue with former ATS Health Equity Fellows
Description:
This interactive fireside chat will feature current and former ATS Health Equity Fellows who will offer insight from their training experience and discuss how the fellowship shaped their careers in respiratory medicine and health equity research. Fellows will reflect on lessons learned, career development strategies, mentorship experiences, and challenges faced while pursuing work in health disparities research. 

The session will also provide practical guidance for prospective applicants interested in the ATS Health Equity and Diversity Fellowship, including advice on preparing competitive applications, identifying mentors, and leveraging fellowship opportunities to build impactful careers focused on health equity. 
 
 Main Learning Objectives: 
- Describe the goals and structure of the ATS Health Equity Fellowship and how it supports early career development in respiratory health equity 
- Identify key strategies for preparing a competitive fellowship application 
- Recognized practical approaches for translating fellowship experiences into impactful research, advocacy, and clinical initiatives

Join a leading allergist for a review of emerging real-world evidence evaluating effectiveness outcomes with triple therapy in adult patients with asthma receiving ICS/LABA. This session will integrate real-world data with current clinical evidence.

Session Name: Evolving Endpoints in Respiratory Trials Moving Beyond FEV1
Description: Join Anthony Bohnert, MD, Executive Director and Therapeutic Area Lead, Respiratory, for an in depth discussion on the evolving landscape of respiratory clinical trial endpoints. Dr. Bohnert will examine how the field is moving beyond FEV1 to embrace more functional, and patient relevant measures. Topics include: Evaluating novel functional endpoints beyond FEV1 Integrating quantitative CT and AI imaging biomarkers into trial design Advancing blood based biomarkers for respiratory disease stratification Leveraging wearable technologies to capture real world respiratory function
