Session Name: NSC13 Optimizing Individual Learning in the Multi-disciplinary ICU: Building Skills & Gaining Competencies
Description: ICU rounds encompass caring for some of the sickest patients while managing procedural responsibilities and difficult conversations. It becomes further challenging when teaching responsibilities are added. Successful strategies for effective bedside teaching include the “one-minute preceptor model” and “retrieval practice”. However, studies have found time pressures and high clinical workload to be significant barriers for faculty to change their teaching styles in the ICU. This can improve by incorporating teaching strategies into the usual workflow of rounds to allow fulfilling of both clinical and educator responsibilities of the attending physician. Another challenge of teaching in the ICU is the presence of multiple learners with a wide spectrum of foundational knowledge and different learning goals. A “single” approach to teaching would not suit the individual needs of such a diverse group. This may call for adoption of novel strategies, often borrowed from fields outside of medical education, such as Differentiated Instruction, to optimize learning for each team member. The Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) expects trainees to obtain competency in six core areas during their course of training. These are patient care, medical knowledge, professionalism, interpersonal communication skills, practice-based learning and improvement and systems-based practice. This session will utilize a novel “multi person role play” format to a) Discuss strategies to balance clinical care and efficiency with educating b) Address needs of different learners and develop strategies for each c) Deliver framework to structure ACGME core competencies into the above strategies.
Location: Learning Studio, Hall C (Level II, OCCC West)

Session Name: B91 INTEGRATING PRAGMATIC CLINICAL TRIALS INTO INTERVENTIONAL PULMONARY OUTCOMES RESEARCH
Description: Advanced diagnostic bronchoscopy and adjunct tools to biopsy pulmonary lesions have rapidly evolved over the last several years. Often, new technologies are rushed to market and integrated into clinical practice despite a paucity of supportive evidence. Particularly, comparative effectiveness and randomized controlled trials have been difficult to execute and given the lack of funding and rapid pace of technologic development, leaving technologies outdated by the time a trial could be completed. This session will discuss the major barriers to randomized controlled trials in advanced bronchoscopy and how pragmatic trials have potential to expedite patient recruitment, study completion, and increase external validity.

Session Name: B82 PRECISION VS PRAGMATISM: STRIKING BALANCE IN THE ICU
Description: Recent critical care research has focused on personalization—using cutting-edge methods to optimize treatment decisions for individual patients. However, work by epidemiologists and implementation scientists consistently demonstrates that we often fall short in delivering evidence-based care for patients with common deadly conditions like sepsis and ARDS. This session will highlight the tension between approaches that seek to personalize care versus those that focus on delivering the best care for populations. Formatted as a series of pro/con-style debates followed by expert discussions, the session aims to move beyond apparent conflict towards an integrated, nuanced approach to important topics in critical care.

Session Name: B90 DECODING BACTERIAL PNEUMONIA: INTEGRATING HUMAN TRIALS, TRANSLATIONAL IMMUNOLOGY, AND NEXT-GEN MODELING TO ADVANCE PRECISION MEDICINE
Description: This session will provide learners with an integrated perspective on bacterial pneumonia by highlighting advances in human clinical studies, immunologic profiling, and innovative modeling systems. Attendees will explore how animal models, organoids, and lung-on-a-chip platforms complement human research and inform therapeutic strategies. Designed for clinicians, scientists, and trainees, the symposium emphasizes the importance of translational approaches in understanding disease mechanisms and developing precision medicine tools. Learners will gain insight into biomarker development, immune responses, and model refinement, with a focus on bridging experimental findings to patient care in pneumonia and sepsis. This session fosters cross-disciplinary learning and collaborative exploration.

Session Name: B87 WHEN TREATMENT HURTS: RETHINKING CPAP IN OBSTRUCTIVE SLEEP APNEA THROUGH A PRECISION MEDICINE LENS
Description: This session will explore why CPAP may not benefit all patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) and may even cause harm in certain subgroups. Learners will gain insight into potential mechanisms of harm, including vascular inflammation, sleep disruption, and loss of cardioprotective intermittent hypoxia. The symposium will emphasize emerging evidence supporting a precision medicine approach to CPAP treatment. Attendees will learn how to apply physiologic phenotyping to identify which patients may benefit the most from therapy. The session will conclude with discussion on future research needs and implications for clinical guidelines and trial design.

Session Name: B85 BEYOND -OMICS: CONNECTING MOLECULAR BIOLOGY TO CELL PATHOPHYSIOLOGY USING SPATIO-TEMPORAL MULTI-MODAL IMAGING
Description: This session will feature exciting, innovative, and cutting-edge research methods in pulmonary basic/translational research. High-yield multimodal imaging methodologies are transforming how we conduct research and our fundamental understanding of pulmonary disease pathogenesis. These advanced imaging techniques address the cellular microenvironment and tissue context, some using real-time spatiotemporal resolution. The talks have broad appeal across different pulmonary diseases (e.g., asthma, COPD, emphysema, ILD, fibrosis, remodeling, pulmonary vascular disease, etc.) and will cover complementary approaches. This aligns with the basic science theme "Understanding the Lung Microenvironment in Disease," and will increase awareness about approaches that will continue to revolutionize pulmonary research.

Topics include evidence-based approaches to care transitions after critical illness, palliative and end-of-life care transitions, tobacco and vaping cessation across the lifespan, and family-centered models of transitional care. Session Name: B88 REWRITING THE CODE: PRECISION DELIVERY VECTORS AND GENE THERAPY FOR PULMONARY VASCULAR DISEASES
Description: This session is designed for clinicians, scientists, and industry professionals interested in gene therapy and delivery vectors for pulmonary vascular diseases. Speakers will highlight current platforms—including viral vectors, intravenous nanoparticles, and targeted peptides—focusing on translational challenges and strategies from bench to bedside. Session Name: B93 LIVING LANDSCAPES: HOW LUNG MICROENVIRONMENTS ORCHESTRATE HOST RESPONSE DURING LUNG INFECTIONS
Description: This session will examine how diverse lung microenvironments influence immune responses, infection outcomes, and tissue repair. Speakers will highlight how viruses, helminths, fungi, and mycobacteria reshape local immune, stromal, and epithelial niches. Topics include type 2 immunity, fibrosis, immunometabolism, and granuloma formation. Session Name: Transforming Care in Bronchiectasis: From Myths to Modern Management
Description:
Secure your spot at NJHealth.org/BronchiectasisCare

1.5 CME/MOC.

Bronchiectasis is a progressive airway disease driven by chronic infection, neutrophilic inflammation, and recurrent exacerbations that significantly impact patients' quality of life. While traditional management strategies remain important, many patients continue to experience disease progression, and the recent approval of the first therapy targeting neutrophil serine protease activity marks a major shift in the treatment landscape.

In this CME dinner symposium and livestream, a panel discussion among expert pulmonologists and infectious disease specialists will help clinicians translate these advances into practice. Panelists will use patient cases to highlight the role of neutrophilic inflammation in disease progression, discuss strategies for recognizing bronchiectasis earlier, and illustrate guideline-based approaches for incorporating newly approved and emerging therapies into individualized treatment plans.

Attendees will gain insight into the scientific rationale for targeting IL-33 in therapeutic development, along with the latest updates from ongoing clinical investigations of biologic agents designed to modulate its activity. Fortunately for patients determined to have RCC, the pharmacologic landscape is evolving, with a variety of novel therapies under development. In this engaging symposium with livestream, leading RCC experts will provide valuable insights related to diagnosis, underlying pathophysiology, and the latest treatment advances on the horizon.
This interactive 1.25-hour session will feature:
 A deep dive into real world insights on the burden of refractory chronic cough, gleaned from a national patient survey
 An interactive gamified differential diagnosis activity, supported by patient testimonials
 Exploration of mechanism of action and the latest clinical data on emerging therapies, featuring an innovative 2D animation that depicts key components of the driving factors underlying RCC
 Interactive polling and live Q&A for direct engagement with faculty

Don't miss this opportunity to enhance your clinical expertise and engage with leading experts to improve the care of your patients with RCC! This activity is accredited for US-based learners only; however, international ATS attendees are welcome to join.

Session Name: NSC15 From A–to–I & 0–to–Omics: An Introductory Field Guide to AI & Omics Research in Lung Diseases
Description: The high-throughput capacity of Omics-based technologies and accelerated application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has expedited our understanding of rare and prevalent pulmonary diseases. However, many health-care related trainees and professionals, particularly in early and mid-career stages, remain intimidated by current taboos surrounding the economic resources and computational infrastructures needed to introduce AI and Omics-based technologies in their lung disease research. To overcome these barriers in early and mid-career members, this session will cover: (1) commonly used Omics-based technologies (array-, sequencing- and mass spectrometry-based), (2) recommendations to pair Omics approaches to basic and clinical research project hypothesis, (3) available public and private AI tools to access and analyze Omics data, (4) strategies for low-code and non-code AI and non-AI-based analysis of Omics data and (5) resources for AI and Omics-based grant mechanisms. This session will feature leaders from the ATS Section of Genetics and Genomics (SGG) who will engage in an Open Forum with a flipped learning approach to learn and discuss potential AI and non-AI Omics-based solutions for the audience's research needs. Hence, this session will foster networking with early career members and ATS SGG to build or expand Omics-based projects that elucidate the pathophysiology of a wide array of lung diseases.

Session Name: NSC16 From Science to Storytelling: How to Use Narratives to Advocate for Change
Description: Clinicians are trained to be experts in the diagnosis and treatment of illnesses, providing high-quality patient care, practicing effective teaching, and conducting quality scientific research. However, most struggle to translate these provider experiences into effective narratives that, when used as an effective political tool, inspire change, mobilize communities, and ultimately drive policy. This interactive workshop being sponsored and led by leaders of state Thoracic Society Chapters will demonstrate how storytelling can be implemented as a powerful advocacy tool. Through case-based examples, participants will learn strategies to transform data and lived experiences into compelling stories that resonate with policymakers, stakeholders, and the public. Participants will practice narrative techniques in small groups, share with large group report outs, and receive feedback to refine their message. By the end of the session, attendees will leave with a concrete framework for crafting stories that integrate evidence and emotion, bridging science and human experience to influence local, regional, and national change. Additionally, local advocacy for health and environmental policy are needed nationwide. There are currently 19 states with official Thoracic Society Chapters. Attendees will learn how to join their state chapter doing work locally, as well as how to start a state Thoracic Society Chapter in their area.

Session Name: C8 SEEING THE DIFFERENCE: USING IMAGING TO DEFINE COPD SUBGROUPS
Description: This session explores how advanced imaging techniques—such as quantitative CT and MRI—are transforming our understanding of COPD heterogeneity. By visualizing structural changes like emphysema, airway remodeling, and small airway disease, imaging allows us to identify distinct patient subgroups that may not be evident through spirometry alone. Session Name: C6 EVOLVING FROM SUBJECTIVE DIAGNOSTIC CATEGORIES TO MOLECULAR ENDOTYPES IN ILD
Description: Current ILD diagnosis relies on subjective interpretation creating artificial boundaries that constrain therapeutic advances. This session demonstrates how molecular technologies can transcend traditional diagnostic categories to identify biologically meaningful endotypes. Speakers present: BAL proteomics revealing molecular convergence across ILD subtypes, endobronchial OCT providing objective microscopic assessment, circulating biomarkers democratizing molecular insights, insights from tissue based-diagnostic tools like cryobiopsy and imaging-molecular integration guiding treatment selection. These complementary approaches offer a pathway from historical nomenclature toward precision medicine, transforming ILD care by matching patients to targeted therapies based on underlying biology rather than subjective classification.

Session Name: C10 PULMONARY REHABILITATION AROUND THE WORLD: LEARNING FROM THE FRONTLINES
Description: Pulmonary Rehabilitation (PR) is standard of care for patients with chronic lung disease. The core components include aerobic exercise training and disease self-management education. Session Name: Early Insults and Lung Trajectories
Description:
Respiratory health in low- and middle-income countries is shaped by exposures and infections that begin in utero and continue across the life course. Adverse antenatal environments, such as maternal malnutrition and exposure to pollutants, can lead to growth restriction and prematurity, impairing lung development and reducing lung function early in life. During infancy and childhood, household and ambient air pollution and recurrent respiratory infections contribute substantially to respiratory morbidity and mortality, with common pathogens causing acute lower respiratory tract infections that increase the risk of asthma, bronchiectasis, and reduced lung function. Both prenatal and postnatal exposures to household air pollution are linked to pneumonia and impaired lung function, and children living in poverty or overcrowded conditions are especially vulnerable. Lung function trajectories established in childhood often persist into adulthood, with early deficits predisposing individuals to chronic respiratory diseases such as asthma and COPD, and a large proportion of adult disease is rooted in early-life exposures including repeated infections, air pollution, tobacco smoke, and poor nutrition. The higher prevalence and severity of these exposures in low- and middle-income settings may explain the lower lung volumes seen even in asymptomatic, non-smoking adults. In adulthood, continued exposure to ambient particulate matter, household air pollution, and tobacco smoke sustains the burden of respiratory disease, with risk patterns differing by age and sex. Effective interventions must therefore target early-life exposures, vaccination, and air pollution reduction, alongside integrated public health strategies that address reproductive, maternal, and child health and environmental risks to prevent chronic respiratory diseases and reduce health disparities.

Session Name: NSC17 Diagnosing and Addressing Learning Disabilities in Trainees
Description: As medicine strives for a more diverse and inclusive workforce, there is an increasing prevalence of medical trainees with learning disabilities. Despite this, many physicians in training feel uncomfortable disclosing known disabilities and asking for appropriate accommodations. Without proper recognition and diagnosis, these learners may not receive the support they need to be successful and face unique challenges. Session Name: MTE31 USE OF SOTATERCEPT IN THE REAL WORLD - WHAT HAVE WE LEARNED SO FAR
Description:
Sotatercept, a first in class activin signaling inhibitor, has revolutionized the management of patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), with several clinical trials showing improvement in important composite clinical endpoints.
However, sotatercept use also comes with the development of potential side effects, such as thrombocytopenia, bleeding, erythrocytosis and telangiectasis, and most recently, also reports of worsening prostacyclin side effects, fatigue, development of intrapulmonary shunts and pericardial effusions. 
In this session, experts in PAH summarize the clinical evidence of sotatercept use, provide data on real world experience and side effect management and review areas of uncertainty in need of further evaluation.
Speakers/Roles: Bernardo, Roberto (Faculty); Sahay, Sandeep (Faculty)
Categories (all): Pulmonary Circulation; Pulmonary Vascular Disease

Session Name: MTE30 MAKING WAVES: OSCILLOMETRY BASICS AND INTERPRETATION FOR CLINICAL AND RESEARCH APPLICATION

Its advantages over traditional pulmonary function testing, specifically effort independence and the ability to detect subtle dysfunction in the smallest airways, make it an attractive adjunct. However, many clinicians are unfamiliar with the performance and interpretation of oscillometry. This session will describe the technique of oscillometry, detail the clinical and research applications of use, and inform practitioners and researchers on approaches to interpretation.
Speakers/Roles: Glick, Danielle Renee. (Faculty)
Categories (all): Medical Education; Asthma; Environmental and Occupational Lung Diseases; Pediatrics; Clinical Problems; COPD

Session Name: MTE37 THE CELLULAR LANDSCAPE OF COPD: NOVEL INSIGHTS FROM GENOMICS AND CELL BIOLOGY
Description: This session will explore the evolving cellular and molecular landscape of COPD through the lens of cutting-edge technologies such as single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, proteomics, and integrative genomic analysis. The discussion will focus on how these approaches are reshaping our understanding of the key cell types, pathways, and regulatory networks that drive disease progression and heterogeneity. Emphasis will be placed on discoveries that challenge traditional paradigms and open new avenues for precision medicine in chronic lung disease. Attendees will gain insight into how multi-level data integration can illuminate novel mechanisms and potential therapeutic targets in COPD.

Session Name: MTE34 TO PNEUMONITIS AND BEYOND: A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW OF DYSPNEA FROM IMMUNE CHECKPOINT INHIBITORS
Description: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are utilized for almost all types of lung cancer. The most well-known pulmonary complication of ICIs is treated-related pneumonitis, but ICIs can also exacerbate COPD, induce reactive airways disorders and sarcoid-like reactions, cause inflammatory changes in the heart (myocarditis), and respiratory muscle weakness (myasthenia gravis, myositis), all of which can cause shortness of breath. As ICIs are increasingly utilized, pulmonologists need to recognize and be familiar with the management for each of these complications that can cause dyspnea, as not all require cessation of potentially effective ICI treatment and immune suppression.

Session Name: NSC18 Legislation, Implementation, Outcomes, and the Path to 50 States: Stock albuterol policies
Description: Asthma is a leading cause of school absenteeism and EMS calls, in part because many students with asthma lack access to bronchodilators during the school day. Stock bronchodilator programs, established through state laws or local regulations, allow schools to keep medication, typically albuterol inhalers and spacers, on hand for emergencies. Use of the stock inhaler results in the student returning to class in more than 75% of instances, preserving learning time and reducing burdens on students, families, and teachers. Stock albuterol legislation is typically bipartisan and popular among constituents and policymakers. ATS members have helped lead successful legislative and implementation efforts across the U.S.; many are involved with local programs or doing research on outcomes and implementation. Stock albuterol policy was the focus of an official ATS Policy statement in 2021. There are currently 26 states with stock albuterol policies, many of which were passed in recent years. This movement is similar to a previous effort regarding stock Epi-Pens for food allergy in schools, which resulted in laws in all 50 states. ATS members are ideally suited to bring this issue to state lawmakers, and this is an excellent model for state health advocacy. The session will include experts in stock bronchodilator policymaking, guidelines, implementation, and research from Texas, Arizona, Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania. Experts will discuss past experiences and share outcomes data, sharing advice related to policymaking and implementation. The session will include a brief presentation and will feature an interactive panel discussion tailored to audience questions and input.

Session Name: From Variability to Validation: Reframing Imaging in Pulmonary Clinical Trials - If imaging is central to pulmonary disease, why isn’t it consistently trusted in clinical trials or by regulators?
Description:
Pulmonary research, particularly in rare and progressive lung diseases, is advancing rapidly, yet clinical trials continue to face persistent challenges in disease characterization, endpoint definition, and outcome interpretation. This session focuses on a less visible but critical issue: variability in disease measurement may be shaping trial outcomes more than we realize.

Across studies and institutions, variability in imaging interpretation, measurement approaches, and endpoint definitions continues to limit its use in clinical trials and regulatory decision-making. Despite its central role in understanding lung disease, imaging has yet to achieve consistent qualification as a biomarker.

Bringing together perspectives from radiology, pulmonology, pathology, and clinical research, this session will examine how variability impacts clinical decision making and trial design, and explore approaches to improve standardization, reproducibility, and biomarker qualification.

This session will also introduce the next phase of work from the Open Source Imaging Consortium (OSIC), including expanded longitudinal datasets and the launch of coordinated, multi-site research through the OSIC Cooperative Research Network (OCRN). As a first example, OCRN is initiating a project focused on the progression from interstitial lung abnormalities (ILA) to ILD, leveraging longitudinal imaging and lung cancer screening cohorts to define early disease signals and progression pathways. Dr. Martina Koziar Vasakova will contribute insights from screening populations, where incidental findings may represent the earliest detectable stages of fibrotic lung disease.

Dr. George Washko will provide context on the evolving role of imaging, while Dr. Lida Hariri will explore links between imaging and underlying biology.

By reframing imaging as a coordinate system for disease, this session outlines a path toward more consistent measurement, improved trial design, and more effective translation into patient outcomes.

Learning Objectives / Key Takeaways
1. Understand how variability in imaging measurement impacts clinical trials and regulatory acceptance
2. Identify key barriers preventing imaging from achieving consistent biomarker qualification in pulmonary disease
3. Explore emerging approaches to improve standardization and reproducibility using longitudinal imaging data
4. Review updates to the OSIC platform, including expanded datasets and a disease-agnostic, shared infrastructure enabling scalable, cross-disease research and regulatory-aligned evidence generation
Speakers/Roles: Koziar Vašáková, Martina (Speaker); Hariri, Lida (Speaker); Washko, George (Speaker); Estes, Elizabeth (Speaker)

Description:
Attendees at this year’s Plenary Session will hear from keynote speaker Rana Awdish, MD, author of the bestselling medical memoir In Shock: My Journey from Death to Recovery and the Redemptive Power of Hope. Her presentation, “After Shock, The Redemptive Power of Hope,” will draw on the evocative power of art as well as her own experience to illustrate how we can reclaim the power that resides in our attention, relationships, and willingness to stay present with suffering long enough for it to transform into something truly healing. 

A member of the ATS for two decades, Dr. Awdish is the medical director of care experience at Henry Ford Health in Detroit, Michigan, and a pulmonary critical care physician. She was named Schwartz Center for Compassionate Healthcare National Compassionate Caregiver of the Year, a U.S. News & World Report Healthcare Hero, and Physician of the Year by Press Ganey in South Bend, Indiana. 

She was finishing a fellowship in critical care when she was rushed to her own training hospital as she experienced a life-threatening miscarriage. She subsequently spent months fighting for her life, enduring consecutive major surgeries and experiencing multiple overlapping organ failures. Her memoir recounts her experience and the surprising lack of compassion from the physicians who treated her. 

The Plenary Session will also include the ratification of the 2026-27 slate of leaders, and remarks from outgoing president Raed A. Dweik, MD, MBA, ATSF, and incoming president Michelle Ng Gong, MD, MS, ATSF.

Session Name: NSC19 Finding Your Team: Networking Across Disciplines for Stronger Science

Yet early- and mid-career professionals often receive little guidance on how to identify collaborators and build sustainable partnerships across disciplines. This interactive session will help participants practice networking and team-building skills. Participants will then engage in hands-on networking activities, including the use of “Ask Me About…” prompts and a Team Finder worksheet, to identify their own expertise, articulate collaboration needs, and connect with colleagues from other backgrounds. Small-group match-ups will allow attendees to brainstorm potential project ideas, share strategies for sustaining partnerships, and leave with new professional contacts. Session Name: NSC21 From Labs to Lungs: Translating Respiratory Science for Impact
Description: Effective science communication is essential for translating research into clinical care and public health policy. We now live in a time where the attack on science and those doing life-saving research threatens the very future of that research and advances in therapies that will save lives. The gap between research and implementation is in part due to ineffective communication of science. Complex physiological concepts, technical jargon, statistical nuances, and evolving evidence bases can be difficult to distill for the public and policymakers. Yet, implementing evidence-based policies and interventions is critical to improving public health. Despite the importance of communicating science, few healthcare providers are well-equipped to do so. Time constraints limit physicians' ability to engage in communication training, physicians and researchers may have limited engagement on social media platforms, and institutional incentives often prioritize publication over public engagement. Additionally, the rise of misinformation requires scientists to compete with simplified but inaccurate messages that spread rapidly through social media. This session will discuss the importance of science communication, barriers to effectively translating science to public and policymakers, and strategies for improving science communication. Learning Objectives: 1. Appraise how effective science communication influences clinical practice adoption, public health policy, and patient decision-making 2. Examine key communication barriers, such as jargon complexity, statistical misinterpretation, and platform-specific constraints, when translating respiratory research 3. Create clear, evidence-based messages about respiratory and critical care health research tailored to specific audiences using appropriate digital and traditional communication channels

Session Name: C84 ENDOTHELIAL DYSFUNCTION IN CRITICAL ILLNESS: FROM MECHANISMS TO THERAPIES
Description: Targeting endothelial dysfunction is an emerging strategy to improve outcomes in critically ill patients with ARDS, sepsis, trauma, and AKI. This session will explore the clinical and translational implications of endothelial injury and activation, including glycocalyx degradation and disruption of the Angiopoietin-Tie2 signaling axis. Speakers will highlight emerging biomarkers and novel imaging techniques available to detect dysfunction, as well as therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring vascular homeostasis. Attendees will gain insight into how advances in endothelial biology are driving a more precise, mechanism-based approach to the diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of critical illness.

Description: Sarcoidosis is a challenging disease with many unknowns. Patients can have a highly variable clinical course and decisions around treatment including whether to initiate therapy, duration of treatment, and choice of agent are often not straightforward. This clinically focused session will review the most recent data, explore the evolving treatment paradigms in sarcoidosis and examine specific challenges in treating patients with sarcoidosis.

Session Name: C89 TAKING PRIDE IN OUR WORK: ADVANCING LGBTQIA2S+ ALLYSHIP THROUGH EDUCATION AND ADVOCACY
Description: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual, two spirit (LGBTQIA2S+) patients face well-documented healthcare disparities rooted in long-standing stigma, socioeconomic and political inequality, and a lack of culturally competent medical providers. The health and wellbeing of LGBTQIA2S+ individuals is under increasing threat under recently expanded anti- LGBTQIA2S+ legislation. This symposium will orient participants on the importance of culturally competent care for LGBTQIA2S+ individuals. After establishing a shared understanding, this symposium will cover more advanced topics, including techniques for creating a safe and inclusive space for all patients and strategies for advocacy for minoritized populations in care, education, and research.

Session Name: C87 ADAPTING TO AN EVOLVING RESEARCH FUNDING ENVIRONMENT: A MULTI-NATIONAL APPROACH
Description: Research is a fundamental part of medicine and the allied health professions. This has traditionally relied on funding from large, objective, neutral funders supporting investigators in non-profit contexts. Recent pullbacks from large funders represent the most significant changes in living memory. What should public health advocates anticipate in terms of impact? How can individual researchers maintain viable programs? What alternatives exist, and how can they be accessed? This session grapples with a question existential to a significant fraction of ATS membership from an informed global perspective. Attendees will leave with a deeper understanding of the current state and future of health and behavioral science research funding.

Session Name: C82 LUNG FIBROSIS ACROSS THE LIFESPAN: EMERGING OPPORTUNITIES FOR INTERVENTION
Description: This session explores key drivers of lung fibrosis across the age span, from environmental and genetic risk factors to cellular and extracellular mechanisms. Talks will highlight how environmental exposures contribute to fibrogenesis and how preventive strategies may mitigate risk; genetic predispositions and advances in gene therapy; the role of epithelial aging and cell death in disease onset; and how targeting fibroblasts and fibrotic matrix may halt progression. Session Name: ATS Storytelling Series 3 Ganesh Raghu, MD, ATSF and Yolanda Mageto, MD, MPH, ATSF
Description:
Everyone has a story to tell. Join us at the Networking Super Center, SpeakEasy, on select days and times to hear how successful ATS members navigated and overcame significant hurdles in their careers. 

Ganesh Raghu, MD, ATSF 

 Dr. Raghu has had a longstanding clinical and scientific interest focused on pathogenesis, diagnosis and management of Interstitial lung diseases(ILD),idiopathic interstitial pneumonia (IIP), Sarcoid, Rheumatological lung diseases, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) in particular. He is an international authority in these disorders. With nearly four decades of pioneering work, Dr. Raghu has, led major clinical trials and NIH-funded research, and chaired several national and international evidence based guidelines for diagnosis and management of ILD . 

 Dr. Raghu has authored 425+ original articles, published in peer reviewed medical journals, and nearly 40 books/book chapters has altogether over 475 publications to date. He is among the “Highly cited Researchers” Essential Science Indicators (ESI) as Highly Cited Papers. *Clarivate Web of Science list (of the world’s population of scientists and scientists Highly Cited Researchers are 1 in 1000) in 2019, 2020, 2021 ,2022 and 2025. 

 At the University of Washington(UW) Medical Center, he currently directs the University of Washington’s Center for ILD ( CILD) as well as directing the WASOG Center for Excellence for Sarcoidosis and Co- Director, Scleroderma clinic. He also served as the Director and Medical Director of the UW Lung transplant program that he initiated, developed and founded in 1991. Following the initiation and founding the UW’s Center for ILD in 2013, he stepped down his administrative and leadership roles of the UW lung transplant program but continues to be the transplant pulmonologist for patients with ILD and remains an active member of the UW Lung transplant program. 

 A dedicated patient advocate, he continues to care for patients at UW Medicine and founded the region’s first pulmonary fibrosis support group, which he has led since 1988. 

Yolanda Mageto, MD, MPH, ATSF 

 Dr. Yolanda N. Mageto is a distinguished pulmonary and critical care physician whose career spans more than three decades of clinical excellence, research leadership, and academic achievement. A graduate of Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, she completed her residency in internal medicine at UT Southwestern and her fellowship in pulmonary and critical care medicine at the University of Washington, where she also earned a Master of Public Health in Epidemiology. 

 Over the course of her career, Dr. Mageto has held faculty positions at the University of Washington, UT Southwestern, and the University of Vermont, where she rose to the rank of full Professor. She currently serves as Professor of Medicine at Texas A&M School of Medicine and as Medical Director of Interstitial Lung Disease at Baylor University Medical Center Dallas — a nationally recognized program she has built and led with distinction. 

 A clinician-investigator with expertise in interstitial lung disease and sarcoidosis, Dr. Mageto has served as principal investigator on numerous clinical trials and contributed to landmark American Thoracic Society guidelines and statements. She is a passionate advocate for diversity, equity, and inclusion in academic medicine and has held leadership roles within the ATS, including service on its Board of Directors. 

 Through years of clinical practice, leadership, and mentorship, she has built a career shaped not only by professional achievement, but also by perseverance through the challenges and pivots that define mid-career growth.

Session Name: Nontuberculous Mycobacteria (NTM) Lung Disease: Advancing Detection, Optimizing Therapy, and Improving Patient Quality of Life
Description:
MLI Dialogues | Nontuberculous Mycobacteria Lung Disease (NTM-LD): Advancing Detection, Optimizing Therapy, and Improving Patient Quality of Life is an educational activity designed for pulmonologists and infectious disease clinicians involved in the care of patients with NTM-LD in the United States. NTM-LD is a rare but serious condition, most commonly caused by Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC), and disproportionately affects patients with underlying lung diseases such as bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and asthmaleading to delayed diagnosis, progressive lung damage, and diminished quality of life.


Unlike traditional lectures, this Dialogues program brings you into the conversation. Through real-time audience interaction, multidisciplinary expert insights, and real-world patient cases, you'll explore the complexities of NTM-LD alongside leading specialists in an engaging, studio-quality format. This expert-led activity will include discussion and audience-driven dialogue as participants will examine current and emerging treatment strategies, including approaches for recurrent infection, and explore how evidence-based therapeutic decision-making can optimize clinical outcomes and improve patient quality of life. Registration link: https://www.mlieducation.org/ats26/

Join us for a CME symposium that moves beyond traditional lectures to deliver an immersive, patient-centered learning experience. Through guided patient journey video stations, interactive polling, case-based discussion, and expert-led debriefs, learners will tackle real-world challenges in PAH diagnosis, risk stratification, and treatment optimization. Featuring complex, real-world PAH cases, this program emphasizes practical clinical decision-making, medication titration and side-effect management, and shared decision-making to improve patient outcomes. Session Name: D4 OPTIMIZING CRITICAL CARE THROUGH LEARNING HEALTH SYSTEMS: COMPONENTS AND CONSIDERATIONS
Description: In this session we will review the potential of ICU learning health systems (LHS) to transform critical care delivery, describe key components of an effective ICU LHS, and provide recommendations to build LHS infrastructure in attendees' own systems. An ICU LHS advances the field by 1) leveraging data generated during routine ICU care to inform knowledge generation, 2) creating a culture of continuous process improvement and 3) embedding effectiveness and implementation research in daily practice. Such systems are critical for seeking equity in our healthcare system, and fulfilling the promise of improved care for all our patients.

Session Name: D5 EMPHYSEMA DECODED: AGING GONE WRONG OR REPAIR GONE MISSING?
Description: This session delves into the cellular and molecular drivers of emphysema, exploring whether the disease is primarily fueled by premature cellular senescence or by a failure of lung tissue regeneration. We will examine emerging evidence from human studies and experimental models that link impaired repair pathways, stem cell exhaustion, and persistent inflammation to alveolar destruction. By understanding the balance—or imbalance—between aging processes and regenerative capacity, we can uncover new therapeutic targets to halt or reverse emphysema progression.

Session Name: D9 THE SCIENCE OF PALLIATIVE CARE IN THE ICU: HIGH HOPES, MIXED RESULTS
Description: This symposium will examine the evolving science of ICU-based palliative care, where interventions often fall short of expectations. Despite strong evidence, improvements in outcomes, especially psychological distress among families, remain limited. Drawing on recent trials and implementation studies, speakers will explore what distinguishes effective strategies, when and how palliative care should be delivered, and why commonly measured outcomes may miss the mark. Emerging models that better reflect the needs of critically ill patients and families will be highlighted. The session will close with a look at future research and implementation priorities to help palliative care fulfill its promise.

Session Name: D7 ENDOTHELIAL HETEROGENEITY IN THE LUNG MICROENVIRONMENT: AGE AND DISEASE PERSPECTIVES
Description: Exciting advancements are shedding light on endothelial heterogeneity in the lungs, revealing the complex landscape of distinct lung endothelial cell subpopulations. However, significant knowledge gaps remain, particularly regarding cell-cell communication and how these interactions shape the lung microenvironment in both developing and mature lungs. In this symposium, we will discuss novel insights into the dynamic interplay between the lung endothelium, considered in its cellular diversity, and resident lung cell populations, we will highlight similarities and differences across the lifespan, and explore potential implications for human health and disease.

Session Name: D6 MEET THE BOS: PHENOTYPES AND PATHWAYS IN BRONCHIOLITIS OBLITERANS SYNDROME
Description: Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS) is a severe and debilitating obstructive airway disease marked by small airway inflammation and fibrosis. While fibrosis is a common outcome, there are crucial differences in the many forms of BOS that merit a nuanced exploration. This session will examine the epidemiology, pathobiology, histology, clinical and radiological manifestations, and treatments for different forms of BOS, including chronic lung allograft dysfunction after lung transplantation, post-hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), and post-infectious BOS. A concluding summary will highlight key similarities and differences, offering practical insights for diagnosis and management.

Session Name: D8 THERAPEUTIC ACUTE INTERMITTENT HYPOXIA: TRANSLATION FROM ANIMAL MODELS TO HUMANS WITH INJURY OR DISEASE
Description: Therapeutic acute intermittent hypoxia (tAIH) is an emerging intervention that applies brief, controlled episodes of low oxygen to stimulate endogenous neuroplasticity. Low-dose tAIH protocols, initially characterized in animal models, are now demonstrating promising results in clinical trials. This session will present evidence that tAIH enhances gait recovery in chronic spinal cord injury and stroke, improves breathing in ALS, and reduces apnea burden in OSA when timed to diurnal rhythm. Attendees will learn the mechanisms, protocols, and patient-specific considerations that underpin tAIH, offering a roadmap for clinical translation and research application in rehabilitation and respiratory care.

Session Name: D3 THE CUTTING EDGE OF TREATMENT FOR NICOTINE ADDICTION: WHAT ALL CLINICIANS SHOULD KNOW
Description: This symposium will educate clinicians on the rapidly evolving landscape of treatment for nicotine addiction. Experts will address key topics including the anticipated approval of cytisinicline, the first new treatment for nicotine addiction in nearly 20 years. Speakers will summarize two recent ATS documents (guideline for the treatment of nicotine dependence in adolescents and young adults, research policy statement on co-use of inhaled nicotine and cannabis) and discuss strategies for addressing nicotine addiction among patients who struggle to quit. This session will equip clinicians with the most up to date information to help their patients in treating nicotine addiction and also empower them to advocate for tobacco control efforts.

Session Name: D2 A TALE OF TWO TRANSPLANTS: THE CONVERGENT PATHS OF CHRONIC LUNG ALLOGRAFT DYSFUNCTION AND PULMONARY GRAFT VERSUS HOST DISEASE
Description: Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome is a highly morbid complication after lung transplant (LT) and hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT), characterized by progressive airway fibrosis and leading to respiratory failure. While sharing clinical and histological similarities, these conditions differ in their triggers, fundamentally caused by immune activation due to self (host versus graft in LT) and non-self (graft versus host in HCT) discordance between donor and recipient. The proposed symposium aims to create cross-pollination between experts in transplant-related pulmonary fibrosis (TPF) through discussion of pathobiology, strategies for earlier detection and risk stratification, and emerging antifibrotic therapies.

Session Name: NSC23 Widen Your Net, Broaden Your Path: Networking and Portfolio Building for Early Career Scientists
Description: For the past 2 years, the Pulmonary Circulation Assembly Women in Pulmonary Vascular Workgroup (WoW) has hosted a trainee/early-career focused mentoring session with a brief presentation from a keynote speaker and 8-10 panelists that provide mentoring in small group formats. Proposed topics include but are not limited to: diversifying your research portfolio, finding collaborators, networking, successfully finding career opportunities and distinguishing yourself from your mentor. Session Name: NSC24 Models and Techniques to Map the Influence of Extracellular Matrix Across the Lung
Description: Extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling drives cell fate changes during lung development, injury, aging, and chronic disease. While ECM has long been considered structural, new technologies now reveal it as an active regulator of repair, regeneration, and disease progression. This Networking Super Center session will highlight complementary tools and models, ranging from hydrogels and scaffolds to precision-cut lung slices (PCLS) and in vivo approaches, that are redefining our understanding of ECM-driven mechanisms in lung aging and disease. Short presentations will showcase innovative strategies to study how matrix composition and mechanics direct epithelial, mesenchymal, and immune cell behavior across diverse contexts: COPD, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), developmental repair, and aging. Following these focused talks, discussion leaders will guide a compare-and-contrast dialogue on which ECM tools are most informative and how integration of these methods can accelerate biomarker discovery and therapeutic development. This interactive format will foster cross-disciplinary connections between basic and translational researchers, offering early-career investigators networking opportunities and practical insights into ECM biology. The session aligns with the mission of the NSC by emphasizing collaboration, emerging technologies, and translational pipelines that advance respiratory research.

Session Name: D85 AIMING HIGHER: THE JOURNEY TOWARD ASTHMA REMISSION
Description: The goals of asthma therapy have been to control symptoms and prevent exacerbations. With the recent advances in asthma therapy (i.e. biologics) there has been an ambition to achieve greater disease control and the belief that clinical remission can be a realistic goal in asthma. Achieving that goal requires an acceptable definition of asthma remission and prospective clinical trials to determine the patient and treatment factors associated with arriving at the goal. This session will discuss current definitions of asthma remission and available evidence on remission, as well as obstacles and challenges in defining asthma remission.

Session Name: D86 LOCATION, LOCATION, LOCATION: INTERCELLULAR COMMUNICATION DRIVING LUNG DISEASE
Description: Intercellular communication is fundamental to lung physiology and pivotal in determining the lung microenvironment. Novel mechanisms underlying how cells within the lung transmits and receives information is an emerging area. Both intrinsic and extrinsic factors such as mechanical forces, environmental exposures, and extracellular vesicles, are powerful cues that influence tissue inflammation, repair, and regeneration. In this session, we intend to discuss novel and emerging concepts in cellular communication with emphasis on signals that promote chronic lung disease. We will also discuss new translational and clinical approaches to leverage mechanisms in cellular communication to establish novel biomarkers for chronic lung disease progression.

Session Name: D81 INNOVATIVE APPROACHES TO IMPROVE LUNG CANCER SCREENING ACCESS AND ADHERENCE
Description: This session will highlight innovative approaches to address access barriers to lung cancer screening (LCS) and adherence to follow-up testing. The session includes speakers from pulmonology, cancer epidemiology, and primary care. Topics will include new evidence for novel approaches to engage a high-risk communities in LCS, the latest studies on innovative strategies at the health-system level to improve adherence to timely evidence-based follow-up, and health policy approaches including emerging evidence and advocacy for guideline modification to expand access to LCS for patient groups with high disease burden.

Session Name: D83 EARTH, WIND, AND FIRE: TRANSLATIONAL LESSONS FROM A CHANGING PULMONARY (MICRO)ENVIRONMENT
Description: From birth through adulthood, environmental exposures play a crucial role in the development of both acute and chronic respiratory diseases. As climate change accelerates and the frequency of manmade and natural disasters increases, the health impacts of these exposures continue to grow. Despite this, the underlying mechanisms and pathophysiology driving the onset of new respiratory conditions—or the worsening of existing ones—remain poorly understood. The goal of this symposium is to spotlight key translational insights from exposure studies, emphasizing both basic science and clinical/translational research. Special focus will be given to understanding the health effects and disease mechanisms associated with occupational and environmental exposures such as wildfires, military deployment, and air pollution.

Session Name: D84 EAT. KILL. SURVIVE. THE MACROPHAGE-NTM STANDOFF
Description: Nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are opportunistic pathogens that cause highly morbid lung disease, particularly in individuals with bronchiectasis. Current treatments are prolonged, toxic, and often fail to eradicate infection. Macrophages are central to NTM clearance but can also serve as a niche for persistence. While most prior research has focused on Mycobacterium tuberculosis, NTM species such as M. avium and M. abscessus exhibit distinct host-pathogen dynamics. This session will highlight emerging insights into macrophage-NTM interactions in the lung and spur discussion for potential host-directed therapies to augment or replace current antimicrobial strategies.

Session Name: D82 THE AGE OF INCLUSION: BUILDING BETTER CRITICAL CARE TRIALS FOR OLDER ADULTS
Description: Up to half of ICU admissions are for older adults (ages 65+), yet critical care trials often exclude older ICU patients. Randomized data addressing this growing demographic is scarce and typically confined to subgroup analysis. Critical care trials also lack data on frailty or multi-morbidity, key determinants of outcomes in the older ICU population. We will discuss interpretation of previously completed trials, addressing how data may be applied to older or more frail adults. We also explore how future trials could better incorporate age, frailty, and multimorbidity in design. Experts will discuss how aging and frailty could be incorporated into heterogeneity of treatment effect, and how outcomes for this population must include not only survival but “what matters most” to older adults.

Session Name: NSC25 Reliable Lung Sounds: Practical AI at the Point of Care
Description: This small-group, hands-on session is a skills and methods workshop on digital auscultation. We open with a brief panel on unmet needs at the point of care, then attendees rotate at their own pace through three to four stations, each led by a moderator, e.g.,: - Hands-on auscultation: listen to de-identified clips; “test your ears”; technique refreshers. - AI in context: how timing/confidence/labels should be interpreted alongside symptoms and exam; common pitfalls and equity considerations. - Clinical decision & documentation: practice crafting clear indication language for imaging/consults; quick cases (“what would you do next?”). - Unmet needs discussion: structured prompts to surface barriers and opportunities in diverse clinical settings. Moderators use scripted questions to stimulate peer-to-peer learning; ideas are captured on a shared board and distilled into a post-session tip sheet for participants. The goal is to help clinicians and scientists compare approaches, strengthen bedside skills, and explore responsible, reproducible use of AI-assisted auscultation in real clinics.

Session Name: MD27 KEY RESULTS OF HYBRID EFFECTIVENESS-IMPLEMENTATION TRIALS INVOLVING ACUTE RESPIRATORY DISORDERS
Description: Inpatients with acute respiratory disorders often do not receive evidence-based interventions that have been shown to improve survival rates and reduce morbidity. Hybrid effectiveness-implementation trials, which simultaneously examine the effectiveness of an intervention and the process of implementation, are crucial for ensuring that evidence-based practices are effectively adopted. To address this need, the NHLBI developed RFA-HL-21-001 to support hybrid effectiveness-implementation trials that focus on clinical and implementation outcomes in inpatient settings. During this session, investigators funded by this RFA will present key results of their trials involving acute respiratory diseases and discuss the challenges associated with implementing evidence-based interventions in everyday clinical practice.

Session Name: MD25 NOVEL TOOLS FOR DIAGNOSIS AND LONGITUDINAL MONITORING OF PULMONARY HYPERTENSION
Description: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) has no cure, the average 5-year patient survival rate is 54% with an increased mortality rate by 1.9% per year. One of the main reasons for this high mortality in PH was due to the difficulty in early diagnosis of PH and accurately monitoring of the therapeutic effects. This session will introduce four NHLBI-funded studies on novel imaging and other noninvasive tools for early and accurate diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring of PH. Specifically, we focus on utilizing xenon MRI, echocardiogram, CT, AI-assist digital stethoscope and EKG technologies for early detection and precision diagnosis and monitoring of PH.

Session Name: MD28 UPDATES FROM THE LUNG HEALTH COHORT (LHC) STUDY
Description: The current framework for investigating respiratory diseases is based on defining lung health as the absence of lung disease. In order to develop a comprehensive approach to prevent the development of lung disease, there is a need to evaluate the full spectrum of lung health spanning from ideal to impaired lung health. The Lung Health Cohort is a community-based cohort study focused primarily on characterizing lung health in 25-35 year olds without diagnosed severe respiratory disease initiated in 2021. This session will present baseline data for this novel epidemiological study.

Session Name: MD26 LUNG MAP PHASE 3- HIGH RESOLUTION MOLECULAR PROFILING OF LUNG DISEASES
Description: The overall goal of LungMAP is to build a molecular and cellular atlas of the human lung to serve as a reference to better understand both normal biology and disease pathobiology. LungMAP Phase 3 aims to utilize the power of single-cell omics and other innovative technologies to identify the pathogenic mechanisms of lung disease at cellular resolution, including cell types critical to disease initiation and progression, aberrant molecular pathways in abnormal and diseased cell states, and targets for novel lung disease therapies. Speakers will describe progress on profiling pediatric and adult diseases using single-cell multiomics, spatial multiomics, and other innovative technology platforms as well as advance data analysis tools

Session Name: MD29 COPDGENE: UNDERSTANDING COPD PROGRESSION AND HETEROGENEITY
Description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a leading cause of death in the United States, is a heterologous syndrome with affected individuals demonstrating marked differences in lung structure, physiology, and other clinical features. Insight into COPD heterogeneity requires comprehensive and longitudinal data to elucidate the genetic, clinical, and radiographic determinants of disease progression. The COPDGene study, with over fifteen years of data, has created the largest longitudinal cohort of well-characterized current and former smokers for respiratory disease research.This session will describe how COPDGene has contributed to a molecular understanding of COPD progression as well as different approaches to identifying COPD phenotypes.

Session Name: NSC26 Survive, Then Thrive: Innovations in Post-ICU Recovery with Team-Based Care
Description: Recovery after critical illness is a small but growing niche in critical care medicine. We seek to highlight innovations in ICU recovery across the multi-professional team. We hope to engage those interested in ICU Recovery, provide tools for those interested in starting or who are working in post-ICU clinics/peer support groups/other interventions, and assist with networking. We have a group of panelists, each of which will speak for 10 minutes about his/her involvement in ICU Recovery. Dr. Carla Sevin is a physician Vanderbilt and has run a post-ICU clinic there for over 13 years. Dr. Jo McPeake is a nurse scientist in the UK who has worked on recovery after critical illness, in particular the impact on families. Dr. Kimberley Haines is a physiotherapist in Australia who has studied ways to improve recovery after critical illness, in particular in regards to patient physical function. Dr. Anna Lewis is a social worker who has worked in a post-ICU and helps lead peer support programs. Dr. Rita Bakhru is a physician at MUSC who has created 2 different post-ICU clinics and researches ways in which to improve recovery after critical illness. She will spend 5 minutes discussing opportunities for collaboration through the CAIRO network. The CAIRO Network (Critical and Acute Illness Recovery Organization) is a group of healthcare professionals across the world who collaborate on ways to improve recovery after critical illness. We will then have 15 minute session where questions from the audience will be solicited.
